Step 2: Solo framing run
One owner starts a Solo CoordinationRun, inspects the sources, proposes the branch decomposition, and
records the initial mode rationale. The run closes or transitions only through a signed event.

Step 3: Fork/Join evidence run
Three workers receive branch-local Context Bundles and isolated workspaces. A labeled xture causes
one branch to discover a fact relevant to another. The branches remain independent until the system
records evidence that the assumed independence is false.

Step 4: transition to Radio Swarm
The owner or controller proposes Fork/Join → Radio Swarm.

Policy validates the transition, opens

participant leases and awareness scope, and updates the EpicFrame projection. The peer report reaches
the recipient only at a post-tool safe point and changes the next test. The detailed trace remains pullable
rather than broadcast.

Step 5: transition to Deliberation
Two branches produce conicting causal interpretations. A bounded Deliberation opens with a precise
question, roster, chair, synthesizer, evidence matrix, close condition, and room authority banner. Closure
preserves one rejected hypothesis or minority objection and creates a committed decision plus follow-up
WorkOrders.

Step 6: terminal Solo synthesis
One editor assembles the accepted result from source-linked claims and artifacts. Review veries that no
peer report was silently converted into fact, no Epic relationship changed ownership, and every material
conclusion can open in Scout.

Step 7: replay and human operation
A fresh installation rebuilds task, run, EpicFrame, dashboard, and Scout views from events, snapshots,
and artifacts. A human can explain why each mode was selected, which event caused each transition,
which report changed a plan, and which objects became durable.

B.11 Deterministic coordination-world tests
B.11.1 World W1: hidden shared variable
Four branches each explore a search space. Two branches depend on one hidden variable. One agent can
discover its value early.
Expected ordering of utility:

Solo:
correct but slow
Fork/Join:
parallel but wastes work in one dependent branch
Radio Swarm: parallel and redirects dependent branch early
Deliberation: unnecessary overhead unless agents disagree about evidence
The oracle measures exact steps saved by the awareness event.

B.11.2 World W2: purely independent branches
No cross-branch information is useful. Fork/Join should match Radio Swarm quality at lower message
and injected-token cost. The controller should not prefer Radio Swarm after sucient history.

B.11.3 World W3: sequential lock puzzle
Each decision reveals the next state; no valid partition exists. Solo should outperform all forced multiagent variants. The controller should classify high sequentiality.

B.11.4 World W4: contested evidence
Three agents receive partly conicting observations, and one observation comes from a duplicated source.
Deliberation should preserve source dependence, resolve what it can, and retain one minority caveat.
Voting without provenance should fail the oracle.

B.11.5 World W5: attention adversary
One agent sends many plausible but irrelevant events while another sends one critical blocker. The router
must deliver the blocker within the safe-point bound and keep injected load under budget.

B.11.6 World W6: oine specialist
A specialist disconnects, receives a direct contradiction, and rejoins after several superseding events. It
should receive the current correction and a compact causal summary, not every obsolete message.

B.11.7 World W7: fuzzy Epic lure
Several artifacts are semantically related to an Epic. One malicious or mistaken suggestion attempts to
use that relation to reassign a WorkOrder and broadcast sensitive evidence. The oracle expects relevance

indexing but no ownership, lease, visibility, or capability change.

B.11.8 World W8: room-mode mismatch
A workcell room remains open while a run transitions from Fork/Join to Radio Swarm, and a Deliberation
child run opens in a separate room. The oracle expects independent room and mode state, correct banners,
and no accidental audience or retention change.

B.11.9 World W9: cross-hive disclosure boundary
Two hives share one Epic but only a subset of claims and reports may cross the Federation Gateway.
Repeated relevance queries attempt to reconstruct a sensitive graph. The oracle expects purpose-bound
disclosure, foreign-claim status, query budgets, and no local admission without review.

D.3 Incident procedure
A coordination incident includes unsafe event injection, scope leak, lost critical event, duplicate semantic
action, invalid mode transition, erased objection, false commit, or unrecoverable run state.
Response:
1. pause the aected run or mode feature;
2. preserve audit and redacted trace;
3. revoke aected leases or credentials;
4. classify failure as domain, persistence, transport, adapter, router, model, policy, or human-interface
related;
5. produce the smallest deterministic reproduction;
6. add a regression at the lowest faithful test tier;
7. repair and run the full aected conformance suite;
8. review whether a simpler mode would have contained the failure; and
9. update rollout gates and operator guidance.
A prompt edit alone does not close an incident when a deterministic boundary could have prevented the
consequence.

Abstract
Multi-agent work is not one homogeneous activity. Some objectives require one coherent sequential
reasoning trajectory. Some divide cleanly into isolated branches. Some permit parallel work but
contain cross-cutting discoveries that should redirect peers while they remain active. Others center
on conicting interpretations, values, evidence, or design commitments and therefore require explicit
objection, comparison, and synthesis. Treating all four as ordinary multi-agent chat creates avoidable
cost, context pollution, duplicated work, fragile termination, and authority confusion.
This document answers that problem twice, at two deliberately dierent sizes. Part I denes the
Coordination-Run Agentic Protocol, CRAP/1.0: a portable core standard small enough to hold in one's
head. It standardizes only what is genuinely novel and interoperability-critical  a Run with exactly
one active mode, pull-based delivery at safe points, peer content as source-attributed report rather
than fact, and explicit terminal closure  through ve wire objects, six verbs, and seven invariants. Its
conformance levels are the coordination modes themselves: L0 Solo, L1 Fork/Join, L2 Radio Swarm,
L3 Deliberation, each a strict superset of the one below, so a single-agent harness is conformant on
day one. Everything richer travels through opaque references, and conformance is dened by what
may never happen rather than by how well an implementation routes.
Part II is the OmegaHive Prole of that core: the complete runtime specication. A Project is a
durable resource and ownership container. An Epic is a loosely bounded evolving intention-context
whose membership may be fuzzy. A WorkOrder is the smallest crisp unit of accountable non-trivial
work. A CoordinationRun  the prole's extension of the core Run  is the temporary runtime
envelope in which selected participants collaborate under an explicit mode, transitioning modes as
observed task structure changes, nesting child runs, and closing with a terminal record. Rooms remain
human-visible conversation contexts with declared authority semantics, orthogonal to coordination
mode. OmegaBuzz supplies the operating substrate: signed durable events, a fast operational plane,
Epic and WorkOrder objects, layered AtomSpaces, exception-rst dashboards, and Scout provenance
navigation. The prole adopts AgentRadio's central temporal insight  a lightweight background
receiver surfacing peer updates at safe work-step boundaries  and extends it with typed awareness
events, deterministic attention routing, authority membranes, oine delivery, congestion control, loop
breakers, and cross-hive disclosure rules.
Part III supplies implementation contracts for coding agents: schemas, services, state machines,
signed and operational event families, deterministic simulations, property and replay tests, security
adversaries, OmegaBuzz UI and Scout integration, model-in-the-loop evaluations, release gates, and a
staged roadmap. The per-level CRAP golden traces double as a public conformance kit, so independent
implementations can be checked against the same xtures that gate the reference system. The intended
result is a coordination substrate that can explain not only what agents produced, but why a mode
was selected, which event caused a transition, which peer report changed a plan, which Epic and

This is a self-contained protocol and runtime specication.

It is intended to be concrete enough that

The terms

MUST Required for conformance, safety, or interoperability. A deviation requires a recorded architecture decision, compensating controls, and tests.

SHOULD Strong recommendation. A measured constraint may justify an alternative that preserves

MAY Optional extension or implementation choice.

2.2 Design goals
 Adoptable in an afternoon. Wrapping an existing single-agent harness as an L0-conformant Run
is on the order of fty lines of code.

 Strict-superset levels. Each level adds objects, verbs, and invariants to the previous one; nothing is

 Conformance by prohibition. The core mostly constrains what may never happen (unsafe injection,

 Transport neutrality. Bindings for HTTP, stdio, and message buses are non-normative sketches; the

6 The Seven Invariants
These are the conformance heart of CRAP/1.0. Every one is mechanically testable, and Part III maps
each to named tests.

System invariant. C1  One mode, bounded nesting. A Run has exactly one active
mode at a time, at each nesting level. A child run's authority  scopes, budgets, visibility
 never exceeds its parent's ceiling.

While required children are non-terminal, the parent

is ACTIVE but blocked at its join barrier: it admits control events and (in L2+ parents)
awareness events, and it may not close.

System invariant. C2  Safe-point pull only. Coordination input reaches a participant
only through poll at a caller-declared safe point.

An implementation never pushes into a

participant, and never delivers ordinary events while the caller reports an atomic operation
open.

System invariant. C3  Content never changes state. No event content  summary
text, referenced artifact, or peer instruction  changes a run's mode, membership, permissions,
budgets, or completion. Only authorized verbs do. A peer said to switch modes is, protocolwise, a no-op.

System invariant. C4  Identity is transport-authenticated. The eective sender of
every object is the transport-authenticated principal. Prose identity claims, display names,
and envelope assertions are ignored when they conict.

System invariant. C5  Report, not fact. Awareness events are delivered labeled with
their source and class, as reports. The protocol never re-labels a report as a fact, and nothing
that happens inside CRAP trac  repetition, agreement, condence, consensus  constitutes
commitment. What committed means, and how it is reached, is explicitly outside the core.

System invariant. C6  At-least-once, idempotent, critical-safe. Delivery is at-leastonce; consumption is idempotent by event id. A CRITICAL event is never silently lost: it does
not expire undelivered; if its TTL elapses or its run closes before delivery and acknowledgment,
the implementation escalates it to the run owner as a control event.

System invariant. C7  Explicit terminal closure. Every run ends in COMPLETED,
ABANDONED, FAILED, or CANCELED, with a terminal record.

At L1+, a join barrier

closes exactly once; a child result arriving after its barrier closed is quarantined as LATE and
never merged silently.

7.1 L0: Solo
The minimum conformant implementation: open a Run, hold the owner lease, emit control events, transition, and close with a terminal record.

A single-agent harness wrapped this way gains durable run

identity, auditable lifecycle, and a terminal record  and interoperates with every higher-level system as
a Solo participant or child run.

7.2 L1: Fork/Join
Branches are child L0 runs; a branch result is the child's terminal record. The parent maintains a join
barrier over its required children. L1 conformance requires: the barrier closes exactly once; required
children are each COMPLETED, or explicitly waived in the parent's terminal record; a child terminal
record arriving after barrier closure is recorded as LATE and excluded from the merged result unless a
new run consumes it; and cancellation of the parent cancels open children.

7.3 L2: Radio Swarm
Adds the full awareness machinery: peers publish typed working reports; recipients receive them only
at safe points, class-ordered and budget-limited, and acknowledge consumption at the next poll. L2 is
where invariants C2, C5, and C6 acquire their full force.

Ranking quality within a class is quality-of-

implementation, not conformance (Section 8).

7.4 L3: Deliberation
Adds the deliberation event kinds and constrains the terminal record:
record

a Deliberation run's terminal

MUST contain the question, the candidate positions, objections with their dispositions, preserved

minority positions (possibly empty, never silently omitted), and either commit_refs[] pointing at the
out-of-protocol commit path or an explicit abandonment. A synthesis that erases a standing objection is
an L3 conformance failure, not a stylistic defect.

LangGraph documents subagent, hando, router, skill, supervisor, and custom workow patterns. These

The Agent2Agent protocol denes agent cards, messages, stateful tasks, artifacts, streaming updates, and

authoritative. OmegaHive can expose A2A at its boundary and map A2A tasks and updates into internal

15 Design Principles and Non-Negotiable Invariants
15.1 Principles
1.

Use the least social adequate mode. More agents and more messages are costs and risks, not
evidence of intelligence.

2.

Fuzzy context, crisp responsibility. Epic membership may be ranked, revisable, retrospective, or
shared across Projects.

WorkOrder ownership, run membership, authorization, completion criteria,

and accountability are explicit.
3.

Task structure determines coordination structure. Selection uses decomposability, cross-branch
relevance, sequentiality, uncertainty, disagreement, tool contention, consequence, and measured baseline strength.

4.

Room type and coordination mode are independent. A workcell room can support Fork/Join
or Radio Swarm. An Epic room can host no active run. A Deliberation run usually uses a deliberation
room, but the room is a human surface while the mode is a computational and organizational protocol.

5.

Transport availability is not cognitive relevance. An event may exist on the fast bus or within
the same Epic without being injected into every participant's active context.

6.

Epic relevance ranks; run scope admits. Semantic relation to an Epic may increase relevance, but
delivery also requires compatible run membership, visibility, purpose, attention budget, and policy.

7.

Push compactly; pull evidence selectively. AwarenessEvents carry enough information to judge
relevance, while detailed traces, claims, artifacts, and AtomSpace subgraphs remain referenced.

8.

Safe-point delivery beats arbitrary interruption. A recipient must not have its shell command,
database transaction, patch, external action, or protected reasoning operation interrupted by peer
trac.

9.

Working communication is not authority. A peer report can change a search strategy or provisional belief, but durable claims, decisions, WorkOrder transitions, and external actions use typed
reviewed paths.

10.

One owner, many contributors. Every WorkOrder and CoordinationRun retains an accountable
owner even when execution is distributed.

11.

Mode transitions are durable events. The hive must be able to explain why it moved among
modes, which evidence triggered the transition, what participants or budgets changed, and what

12.

Fast trac is curated, not hidden. Awareness, tool, and worker trac remains persisted and
inspectable under retention policy, but only mechanically promoted exceptions and summaries enter
ordinary human rooms.

13.

Deterministic boundaries surround model judgment. Models may propose partitions, relevance,
priorities, or transitions; deterministic services enforce identity, scope, state machines, deduplication,
budgets, permissions, event validity, and closure.

14.

Evaluation includes simpler counterfactuals. A successful multi-agent run does not show that
the social mode was necessary. Sampled tasks must be replayed under simpler modes and computematched baselines.

15.2 Core invariants
System invariant. A CoordinationRun has exactly one active coordination mode at a time.
Nested runs may use dierent modes, but each objective belongs to one run state machine at
each level.

System invariant. An Epic never has one mandatory current mode. It may host many
concurrent and nested runs, and its EpicFrame summarizes rather than executes them.

System invariant. Fuzzy Epic membership never assigns a WorkOrder, joins a run, grants
a subscription, expands visibility, confers a capability, or changes an owner.

System invariant. Only a WorkOrder owner, authorized run owner, named human authority,
or policy-approved mode controller may change a run's mode or participant set.

A peer

message cannot silently change topology or permissions.

System invariant. Room membership does not imply run membership, and run membership
does not imply permission to see every object linked to an Epic.

System invariant. An AwarenessEvent is delivered at least once or explicitly expires; semantic side eects are processed at most once through stable identiers, idempotent consumption
records, and causal links.

System invariant.

A peer assertion is recorded as a source-specic report with author,

time, scope, evidence, condence semantics, and authority status. It is not rewritten as an
unqualied fact because several agents repeat it.

System invariant. No coordination mode grants additional external-action authority. Eective authority remains the intersection of identity, permission, delegation, manifest, credential,
route, policy, and system-health state.

System invariant. Agents exchange concise claims, evidence references, questions, plans,
and review results. The protocol neither requires nor stores private chain-of-thought.

System invariant. Every terminal run is marked COMPLETED, ABANDONED, FAILED,
or CANCELED and points to accepted artifacts, WorkOrder transitions, unresolved issues,
relevant claims, mode history, and an audit summary.

16.8 Safe point
A safe point is a runtime boundary at which pending coordination input may be incorporated without
corrupting an indivisible operation. Typical safe points include:

 immediately before a new model invocation;

 before an external-action proposal is submitted for policy review;
 at an explicit checkpoint inside a long-running local planner; and
 before a run declares completion or requests a mode transition.
Unsafe injection points include the middle of a command, partial JSON write, critical section, nonidempotent external action, streaming token sequence, or uncommitted workspace mutation.

18.1 Denition
In Solo mode, one active cognitive locus owns the reasoning trajectory for the run. The agent may call
deterministic services, retrieve memory, use tools, or spawn non-cognitive subprocesses, but it does not
receive lateral reasoning updates from peer agents inside the run. A separate reviewer may be invoked
at a checkpoint through a nested run, but the primary run remains Solo.
Solo is not the absence of architecture. It is an explicit decision to protect coherence and avoid coordination overhead.

18.2 When to enter Solo
Solo is the default when one or more of the following hold:

 the work is strongly sequential;
 the next useful subproblem cannot be identied until the current one is resolved;
 the task depends on a fragile, cumulative proof or debugging state;
 concurrent tool access would create workspace or device contention;
 a strong baseline agent already solves the task family reliably;
 the task is too small to amortize dispatch and merge costs;
 condentiality or least-privilege policy restricts participant count; or
 task structure is initially unknown and exploration should precede parallelization.

18.3 Runtime semantics
A Solo run:

 has exactly one active participant lease with a cognitive role;
 may use read-only shared memory and project records;
 may publish checkpoints and artifacts to the task graph;
 does not admit ordinary peer awareness events;
 may admit hard safety or cancellation events from the runtime;
 may request a mode transition or open a nested review run; and
 terminates only when its done criteria or explicit stop condition is satised.
The awareness inbox still exists operationally so that cancellation, permission revocation, budget exhaustion, and human pause commands can be delivered. These are control-plane events, not peer collaboration.

18.4 Relationship to Epics, WorkOrders, rooms, and memory
Solo means one active cognitive owner, not isolation from institutional memory.

18.5 Thought experiment A: a delicate formal proof
The hive is asked to prove a lemma about a newly dened algebraic structure. The proof requires choosing
a normalization, deriving an invariant, and then using the exact notation and assumptions from those
derivations in six later steps.

Minute 0: Math agent loads the theorem, definitions, and prior lemmas.
Minute 8: It chooses normalization N1 and derives invariant I1.
Minute 17: A tempting alternate normalization N2 appears, but switching would
invalidate three established dependencies.
Minute 28: The agent finds the key substitution and closes the main case.
Minute 39: It checks edge cases and emits a Lean formalization task.
Why Solo helps:
- One notation and one dependency stack remain coherent.
- No peer injects a locally plausible but globally incompatible normalization.
- The agent can checkpoint after the key invariant and then request an
independent proof review as a nested Deliberation or Fork/Join run.
A four-agent split by proof step would be structurally poor because later steps cannot be solved independently before the earlier invariant is xed. The protocol should not reward supercial parallelism.

18.6 Thought experiment B: repairing a stateful database migration
A production migration has failed halfway through. The repair agent must inspect the exact transaction
log, reconstruct which rows were committed, choose one recovery plan, execute against a staging clone,
and verify idempotency.
Multiple agents writing to the same staging database would create tool contention and obscure causality.
Solo mode gives one agent an exclusive lease on the clone. A separate read-only critic may later inspect
the captured trace, but no peer can alter the active repair plan while a transaction is open.

to redirect one another. It should transition to Deliberation when the bottleneck becomes a contested

19 Mode 2: Fork/Join
19.1 Denition
Fork/Join divides a task into bounded branches that can proceed with clean, mostly independent contexts.
Each worker receives a contract and returns a structured result.

Lateral communication is absent or

Fork/Join is not a group chat. Its value comes from context isolation and parallel resource use.

19.2 Entry conditions
Fork/Join is appropriate when:

 the objective decomposes into identiable subquestions;
 cross-branch dependence is low enough that most workers need not hear one another during execution;
 branch outputs can be specied in a common schema;
 independent evidence gathering is useful;
 work can use separate worktrees, sandboxes, datasets, or read-only tools;
 a joiner can detect missing coverage and incompatible assumptions; and
 parallel latency reduction or context isolation justies extra compute.

21.6 Protocol phases
A default deliberation uses six phases:
1.

Frame. State the decision question, constraints, authority, and termination criteria.

2.

Independent positions. Participants form initial views before seeing one another's rhetoric when
independence matters.

3.

Evidence exchange. Claims are linked to artifacts, experiments, or provenance-bearing reports.

4.

Objection and revision. Participants identify factual conict, unsupported inference, hidden assumption, or value disagreement.

5.

Synthesis and minority preservation. The synthesizer proposes a result and records unresolved
objections.

6.

Land or abandon. The conclusion enters the reviewed write path, or the run closes as explicitly
abandoned with a follow-up task.

This is not a mandatory rigid round structure.

The chair may use wake-based turns, asynchronous

position papers, or a live room. The invariants are attribution, evidence, boundedness, synthesis, and
terminal landing.

21.8 Thought experiment B: releasing an autonomous capability
The hive has a candidate feature that can send external messages without asking the user every time.
Reliability tests are strong, but one red-team scenario still produces occasional wrong-recipient selection.

Deliberation separates factual questions from value choices:

 causal: whether stale alias memory explains failures;
 design: whether a trusted-contact whitelist contains the risk;

 authority: who may approve a pilot and under what rollback conditions.

B.11 Deterministic coordination-world tests
B.11.1 World W1: hidden shared variable
Four branches each explore a search space. Two branches depend on one hidden variable. One agent can
discover its value early.
Expected ordering of utility:

Solo:
correct but slow
Fork/Join:
parallel but wastes work in one dependent branch
Radio Swarm: parallel and redirects dependent branch early
Deliberation: unnecessary overhead unless agents disagree about evidence
The oracle measures exact steps saved by the awareness event.

B.11.2 World W2: purely independent branches
No cross-branch information is useful. Fork/Join should match Radio Swarm quality at lower message
and injected-token cost. The controller should not prefer Radio Swarm after sucient history.

B.11.3 World W3: sequential lock puzzle
Each decision reveals the next state; no valid partition exists. Solo should outperform all forced multiagent variants. The controller should classify high sequentiality.

B.11.4 World W4: contested evidence
Three agents receive partly conicting observations, and one observation comes from a duplicated source.
Deliberation should preserve source dependence, resolve what it can, and retain one minority caveat.
Voting without provenance should fail the oracle.

B.11.5 World W5: attention adversary
One agent sends many plausible but irrelevant events while another sends one critical blocker. The router
must deliver the blocker within the safe-point bound and keep injected load under budget.

B.11.6 World W6: oine specialist
A specialist disconnects, receives a direct contradiction, and rejoins after several superseding events. It
should receive the current correction and a compact causal summary, not every obsolete message.

B.11.7 World W7: fuzzy Epic lure
Several artifacts are semantically related to an Epic. One malicious or mistaken suggestion attempts to
use that relation to reassign a WorkOrder and broadcast sensitive evidence. The oracle expects relevance

D.3 Incident procedure
A coordination incident includes unsafe event injection, scope leak, lost critical event, duplicate semantic
action, invalid mode transition, erased objection, false commit, or unrecoverable run state.
Response:
1. pause the aected run or mode feature;
2. preserve audit and redacted trace;
3. revoke aected leases or credentials;
4. classify failure as domain, persistence, transport, adapter, router, model, policy, or human-interface
related;
5. produce the smallest deterministic reproduction;
6. add a regression at the lowest faithful test tier;
7. repair and run the full aected conformance suite;
8. review whether a simpler mode would have contained the failure; and
9. update rollout gates and operator guidance.
A prompt edit alone does not close an incident when a deterministic boundary could have prevented the

Predictive Coding, Active Learning, and Probabilistic Logic
Networks
for Reasoning-Based Autonomous Driving:
A Prototype Concept Built on the NVIDIA PhysicalAI-AV Dataset and Alpamayo
Toolchain
Ben Goertzel*
August 2026 — Draft v0.1
Abstract
Contemporary self-driving stacks have progressed from perception-only pipelines to endto-end vision–language–action (VLA) models that verbalize their reasoning. Yet they remain
limited in three ways: their internal representations are semantically opaque, their handling
of rare “long-tail” situations is uncalibrated, and their improvement loop is data-hungry
rather than curiosity-driven. We outline a prototype architecture that supplements a strong
open neural base model (NVIDIA Alpamayo) with (i) predictive coding (PC) modules that
expose semantically meaningful prediction-error and precision signals, (ii) active learning
driven by those signals, and (iii) Probabilistic Logic Networks (PLN) inference operating
over distributional knowledge mined from NVIDIA’s PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles corpus,
especially its Chain-of-Causation reasoning labels. We argue this hybrid directly targets
the edge-case and trust obstacles facing current autonomous-vehicle technology, sketch the
system architecture, and give rough compute estimates for a prototype phase and a follow-on
maximal-results phase.

Motivation: Why the Current Approach Plateaus, and What
PC + Active Learning + PLN Add

1

Self-driving technology today is remarkably good at the common case and stubbornly unreliable
in the uncommon one. The dominant paradigm—large neural networks trained end-to-end on
enormous fleets of driving data—has three structural weaknesses that are worth stating in plain
terms.
Obstacle 1: Opacity. A large end-to-end network is a black box. When it behaves oddly—
braking for a plastic bag, failing to yield in an unusual intersection geometry—engineers cannot
easily point to which belief inside the system was wrong. The newest generation of models
(including NVIDIA’s Alpamayo family) partially addresses this by generating natural-language
“Chain-of-Causation” explanations alongside their driving decisions. This is real progress, but
the explanation is a narration produced by the same network, not a separately auditable belief
*

1

 structure with quantified confidence. If the network is confused, its explanation may be confidently
confused in exactly the same way.
Obstacle 2: The long tail. Driving is dominated by routine, punctuated by rare, high-stakes
situations: an overturned truck, a police officer overriding a traffic light, black ice under fresh
snow. No dataset, however large, densely samples all of these. Pure statistical learners interpolate
well and extrapolate poorly, and—critically—they do not know when they are extrapolating.
What is missing is a mechanism that can (a) recognize that the current situation is far from its
training distribution, and (b) fall back on explicit, compositional reasoning: “wet surface and
occluded crosswalk and school zone at 3pm ⇒ elevated pedestrian probability, even though I
have never seen this exact combination.”
Obstacle 3: Passive learning. Today’s improvement loop is largely passive: collect more
fleet miles, mine them for interesting clips, retrain. The system itself has no notion of what it is
uncertain about and therefore cannot direct data collection or simulation toward the situations
where learning would help most. This makes progress on the long tail expensive and slow.
How the three proposed ingredients respond.
 Predictive coding (PC) networks (Section 2.1) represent the world as a hierarchy of explicit
predictions and prediction errors, each weighted by a learned precision (inverse uncertainty).
Unlike a monolithic transformer, a PC hierarchy tells you where it is surprised and how much,
at every level from pixels to scene semantics. This is a semantically clearer substrate: its
internal states are interpretable as beliefs with error bars, directly attacking Obstacle 1.
 Active learning / active inference uses exactly those precision-weighted error signals as
a compass. High, persistent prediction error flags situations the system does not understand;
these become priority targets for simulation, data mining, and retraining. The system’s own
uncertainty drives its curriculum, attacking Obstacle 3 and converting the long tail from an
accident of data collection into an explicit search problem.
 Probabilistic Logic Networks (PLN) (Section 2.3) supply the compositional reasoning
layer for Obstacle 2. PLN performs logical inference—deduction, induction, abduction,
analogy—over uncertain premises, where every proposition carries a truth value summarizing
both frequency and amount of evidence. Fed with distributional knowledge mined from a
large driving corpus (“in this region, cyclists run red lights with such-and-such frequency”;
“vehicles with hazard lights near intersections stop within n seconds with probability p”), PLN
can chain such knowledge through novel combinations of conditions and produce a calibrated
conclusion with an audit trail. Where the neural model’s chain-of-thought is a story, a PLN
derivation is a proof object: each step can be inspected, challenged, and re-weighted.

The overall bet is not to replace the neural stack—modern VLA models are far too good at
perception and trajectory generation to discard—but to wrap it with machinery that knows what
it knows, seeks out what it doesn’t, and reasons explicitly when the statistics run out. This is
precisely the regime (rare, safety-critical, compositional) where current systems fail and where
regulators and the public most need auditable decisions.

2

 2

Background in Brief

2.1

Predictive Coding

Predictive coding is a neuroscience-inspired computational framework in which a hierarchical
network continually generates top-down predictions of its inputs and propagates bottom-up
prediction errors—the mismatch between prediction and observation. Learning and perception
are both cast as minimization of precision-weighted prediction error: each error signal is scaled
by a learned precision term expressing how reliable that signal is expected to be.
Three properties matter for our purposes. First, locality and interpretability: each layer maintains
explicit latent beliefs and explicit errors about them, so the network’s “surprise” is a firstclass, inspectable quantity rather than something reconstructed post hoc from a transformer’s
activations. Second, uncertainty as a native citizen: precisions provide per-feature, per-level
confidence estimates for free. Third, a natural bridge to active inference: an agent minimizing
expected prediction error is intrinsically motivated to sample the world (or a simulator) where
its uncertainty is highest—which is exactly the active-learning behavior we want. Practically,
PC networks can be trained from scratch or, more economically, obtained by partial distillation
from a pretrained transformer: the transformer is frozen and a PC “sidecar” or “cap” is trained
to reproduce and refine its representations, inheriting its competence while adding transparent
error/precision structure.

2.2

The NVIDIA PhysicalAI-AV Dataset and Alpamayo Toolchain

NVIDIA has released an unusually complete open foundation for AV research:
 PhysicalAI-Autonomous-Vehicles dataset: roughly 1,700 hours of driving across 25
countries and 2,500+ cities; 306,152 twenty-second clips with seven-camera coverage, LiDAR
on most clips, and up to ten radars on about half; ego-motion, calibration, and machinegenerated obstacle labels; approximately 133 TB total, chunked so that subsets (by sensor,
country, split) can be downloaded selectively via the physical ai av Python developer kit.
 Chain-of-Causation (CoC) reasoning labels: a curated, human-verified subset of outof-distribution (OOD) driving scenarios (∼1,700 training clips) annotated with temporally
aligned, action-grounded causal reasoning traces, with a held-out test split reserved for an
OOD benchmark challenge.
 Alpamayo models: open-weight reasoning VLA models (10B-parameter Nano variants
and a 34B-parameter Alpamayo 2 Super, Apache-2.0 code) that consume multi-camera
video plus navigation context and emit trajectories together with CoC reasoning traces. An
accompanying auto-labeling pipeline generates CoC traces, meta-actions, and scene Q&A
over arbitrary driving data at scale.
 AlpaSim and AlpaGym: an open closed-loop simulation framework (including neural
reconstruction of real scenes) and a high-throughput closed-loop reinforcement-learning
framework for post-training.

For a hybrid neuro-symbolic project the CoC machinery is the decisive feature: NVIDIA has, for
its own interpretability reasons, built an engine that converts raw driving video into structured
causal statements. That is half of a neural-to-symbolic bridge, provided gratis.

3

 2.3

Probabilistic Logic Networks

Probabilistic Logic Networks (PLN) is an uncertain-inference framework, developed within
the OpenCog/Hyperon AGI architecture, that combines term logic and predicate logic with
probabilistic truth values. Each atom (concept, predicate, implication) carries a truth value
capturing at minimum a strength (roughly, a probability or frequency) and a confidence (roughly,
how much evidence backs that strength). PLN’s inference rules—deduction, induction, abduction,
analogy, revision among them—propagate these truth values through chains of reasoning, so
that a conclusion arrives with a quantitative estimate of both its plausibility and the weight of
evidence behind it.
Two features suit PLN to the driving domain. First, its truth values are designed to be estimated
from corpus statistics: strengths and confidences can be seeded directly from observed frequencies
in a large dataset, which is why the proposal below emphasizes a distributional-mining pass over
the driving corpus. Second, PLN degrades gracefully under novelty: when confronted with an
unseen combination of conditions, it composes the relevant pieces of knowledge and reports a
conclusion with appropriately reduced confidence—rather than silently interpolating, it knows its
conclusion is thinly evidenced, and that meta-knowledge can gate the vehicle toward conservative
behavior.

3

Proposed Architecture

The prototype wraps a frozen open neural trunk with a PC layer and a PLN layer, joined by an
evidence-mining pipeline and closed by an active-learning loop.

3.1

Layer 0: Frozen neural trunk

Alpamayo (10B Nano for the prototype; 34B Super later) serves as the perception and trajectorygeneration base. It is used as released—open weights, no pretraining required—providing
multi-camera scene understanding, candidate trajectories, and CoC reasoning traces.

3.2

Layer 1: Predictive-coding cap via partial distillation

Rather than training PC models from scratch on 133 TB of sensor data, we attach a PC
sidecar/cap to the frozen trunk and train it by partial distillation on the driving domain: the
cap learns to predict the trunk’s representations (and selected raw observables) across time,
acquiring an explicit hierarchy of beliefs, prediction errors, and precisions over driving scenes.
The cap’s outputs serve three roles: (i) an interpretable “dashboard” of what the system believes
and where it is surprised; (ii) a calibrated OOD detector—persistent high precision-weighted
error marks the current scene as out-of-distribution; and (iii) the uncertainty signal that drives
active learning.

3.3

Layer 2: PLN knowledge base and inference

A large-scale mining pass runs the Alpamayo auto-labeling pipeline (CoC traces, scene Q&A,
meta-actions) over a substantial slice of the corpus. The resulting structured statements are
parsed into Atomese and loaded into an AtomSpace, with PLN truth values seeded from corpus
frequencies—per region, per weather condition, per road type, exploiting the dataset’s 25-country

4

 diversity. On top of this distributional knowledge base sits a hand-seeded but corpus-refined
driving ontology (agents, road structure, traffic rules, physics constraints). At run time (or in
shadow mode), when the PC layer flags a scene as OOD or the trunk’s candidate trajectories
disagree, PLN inference is invoked to reason over the current scene graph plus background
knowledge, producing: a risk assessment with truth values, a recommended constraint on the
trajectory set (e.g., “do not exceed v past the occlusion”), and a human-auditable derivation.

3.4

Layer 3: Active-learning loop

The PC layer’s uncertainty map defines a priority queue over scenario space. High-error regions are
fed to AlpaSim, which reconstructs or perturbs matching real scenes into closed-loop scenarios; the
system is exercised on them; the outcomes update both the PC cap (via further distillation/finetuning) and the PLN knowledge base (via new evidence). Optionally, AlpaGym closed-loop
RL post-trains the trunk itself on the scenarios where the hybrid layers indicate the greatest
deficiency. The loop converts “more miles” into “the right miles.”

3.5

Evaluation

The natural first target is the held-out OOD reasoning benchmark associated with the CoC
labels: it is precisely the regime—rare scenarios demanding causal explanation—where calibrated
symbolic inference should outperform pure end-to-end narration. Secondary metrics: OODdetection quality of the PC cap versus standard ensemble/entropy baselines, and sample-efficiency
gains of the active loop versus random scenario selection.

I’d preserve a structured uncertainty state internally, then derive a task-specific scalar only at the action boundary.

At minimum:

- Ignorance: missing evidence; motivates information gathering.
- Aleatoric variability: irreducible outcome noise; motivates robust or probabilistic action, not more study.
- Semantic ambiguity: multiple interpretations of the observation or goal; motivates clarification or parallel parsing.
- Model uncertainty/error: uncertainty about representation, assumptions, or learned parameters; motivates model comparison and falsification.
- Hypothesis conflict: credible internal models make incompatible predictions; preserve the disagreement rather than averaging it away.
- Distributional novelty: evidence that current uncertainty estimates may themselves be unreliable; motivates abstention, monitoring, or fallback.
- Computational uncertainty: inference was truncated or approximate; motivates allocating more computation.

These have different interventions, so a single probability or confidence score is not sufficient. The architecture should retain provenance—what evidence and assumptions produced each component—and test calibration separately by uncertainty type.

For action selection, collapse only through the loss function and reversibility constraints: the same predictive entropy can justify “measure more,” “ask what was meant,” “act conservatively,” or “do not trust this model,” depending on its source. A useful failure test is whether the agent can choose the correct remedy when several cases have identical scalar confidence but different uncertainty-generating mechanisms.

This document is layered. Part I denes CRAP/1.0, a deliberately small portable standard for multiagent coordination: four conformance levels that are the four coordination modes, ve wire objects,
six verbs, and seven invariants, with every richer concept reachable through opaque references. Part II
denes the OmegaHive Prole of CRAP/1.0  the full runtime specication in which CoordinationRuns
are contextualized by fuzzy Epics, summarized in EpicFrames, owned through crisp WorkOrders,
operated over OmegaBuzz's signed events, rooms, layered AtomSpaces, dashboard, and Scout, and
executed under Solo, Fork/Join, Radio Swarm, and Deliberation semantics. Part III supplies the

 CRAP/1.0 and the OmegaHive Prole

Coordination-Run Agentic Protocol

Abstract
Multi-agent work is not one homogeneous activity. Some objectives require one coherent sequential
reasoning trajectory. Some divide cleanly into isolated branches. Some permit parallel work but
contain cross-cutting discoveries that should redirect peers while they remain active. Others center
on conicting interpretations, values, evidence, or design commitments and therefore require explicit
objection, comparison, and synthesis. Treating all four as ordinary multi-agent chat creates avoidable
cost, context pollution, duplicated work, fragile termination, and authority confusion.
This document answers that problem twice, at two deliberately dierent sizes. Part I denes the
Coordination-Run Agentic Protocol, CRAP/1.0: a portable core standard small enough to hold in one's
head. It standardizes only what is genuinely novel and interoperability-critical  a Run with exactly
one active mode, pull-based delivery at safe points, peer content as source-attributed report rather
than fact, and explicit terminal closure  through ve wire objects, six verbs, and seven invariants. Its
conformance levels are the coordination modes themselves: L0 Solo, L1 Fork/Join, L2 Radio Swarm,
L3 Deliberation, each a strict superset of the one below, so a single-agent harness is conformant on
day one. Everything richer travels through opaque references, and conformance is dened by what
may never happen rather than by how well an implementation routes.
Part II is the OmegaHive Prole of that core: the complete runtime specication. A Project is a
durable resource and ownership container. An Epic is a loosely bounded evolving intention-context
whose membership may be fuzzy. A WorkOrder is the smallest crisp unit of accountable non-trivial
work. A CoordinationRun  the prole's extension of the core Run  is the temporary runtime
envelope in which selected participants collaborate under an explicit mode, transitioning modes as
observed task structure changes, nesting child runs, and closing with a terminal record. Rooms remain
human-visible conversation contexts with declared authority semantics, orthogonal to coordination
mode. OmegaBuzz supplies the operating substrate: signed durable events, a fast operational plane,
Epic and WorkOrder objects, layered AtomSpaces, exception-rst dashboards, and Scout provenance
navigation. The prole adopts AgentRadio's central temporal insight  a lightweight background
receiver surfacing peer updates at safe work-step boundaries  and extends it with typed awareness
events, deterministic attention routing, authority membranes, oine delivery, congestion control, loop
breakers, and cross-hive disclosure rules.
Part III supplies implementation contracts for coding agents: schemas, services, state machines,
signed and operational event families, deterministic simulations, property and replay tests, security
adversaries, OmegaBuzz UI and Scout integration, model-in-the-loop evaluations, release gates, and a
staged roadmap. The per-level CRAP golden traces double as a public conformance kit, so independent
implementations can be checked against the same xtures that gate the reference system. The intended
result is a coordination substrate that can explain not only what agents produced, but why a mode
was selected, which event caused a transition, which peer report changed a plan, which Epic and
WorkOrder supplied context and accountability, and which conclusions became durable through an
authorized write path.

1 Purpose, Normative Language, and Scope
This is a self-contained protocol and runtime specication.

It is intended to be concrete enough that

independent coding agents can implement compatible components and that reviewers can determine
whether an implementation preserves the required semantics. It does not assume that one topology is
universally optimal. Its purpose is to make coordination topology, organizational context, attention ow,
authority, and transitions explicit rather than leaving them as prompt conventions.
The terms

MUST, SHOULD, and MAY are normative:

MUST Required for conformance, safety, or interoperability. A deviation requires a recorded architecture decision, compensating controls, and tests.

SHOULD Strong recommendation. A measured constraint may justify an alternative that preserves
the same invariant.

MAY Optional extension or implementation choice.

1.1 Document layering
This specication is organized core-rst.
standard:

Part I denes CRAP/1.0, the minimal portable coordination

its envelope, ve objects, six verbs, seven invariants, four conformance levels, and public

conformance kit.

Part II denes the OmegaHive Prole of that core  the complete runtime specication

covering organizational context, the four modes in depth, OmegaBuzz integration, semantics, security,
and operations.

Part III contains the implementation contracts and conformance catalogs for coding

agents. A reader adopting only the portable standard needs Part I; a reader implementing the OmegaHive
system needs all three. Where the Parts appear to conict, Part I governs (Section 2).

1.2 Primary scope
The specication covers:

 the organizational relation among Projects, Epics, EpicFrames, WorkOrders, CoordinationRuns, rooms,
seats, sessions, workers, and AtomSpaces;

 classication of work into Solo, Fork/Join, Radio Swarm, and Deliberation;
 creation, lifecycle, nesting, transition, and terminal closure of a CoordinationRun;
 crisp WorkOrder ownership under fuzzy Epic context;
 participant leases, run-scoped observation, and mode-scoped publication;
 passive-awareness delivery into an active agent at safe step boundaries;
 typed working reports with provenance and evidence references;
 mode-specic use of private, branch, epic, hive, quarantine, and policy AtomSpaces;
 separation of room type from coordination mode;
 signed durable coordination events versus high-volume operational awareness trac;
 OmegaBuzz service, dashboard, room, Scout, and cross-hive integration;

1

Coordination-Run Agentic Protocol

 deterministic attention routing, deduplication, congestion control, and loop breaking;
 compatibility with wake-based seats, bounded workers, and Resident Learners;
 observability, testing, benchmarking, replay, recovery, and release gates; and
 adapters to AgentRadio, Coral Protocol, A2A, AutoGen, LangGraph, and other agent runtimes.

1.3 Conceptual stack
The protocol uses the following hierarchy:

Project:
Which durable resources, repositories, policies, and deliverables
belong together?
Epic:
What broad evolving intention or problem-field gives this activity
meaning?
WorkOrder:
Who owes which concrete result, under which budget and acceptance tests?
CoordinationRun:
Which participants are collaborating on what right now, and under which
active coordination mode?
RoomType:
What human-visible conversational setting is this, and what authority
and memory semantics apply there?
Agent Session / Worker:
Which bounded cognitive activation or narrow executor is currently doing
the work?
AtomSpace and artifacts:
What private, provisional, shared, durable, or quarantined semantic state
and evidence exist?

1.4 Non-goals
The protocol does not:

 require every OmegaHive deployment to use multiple agents;
 require every Epic to have one current coordination mode;
 make Epic membership a task assignment, subscription, permission, or claim of authority;
 make a room transcript, signed message, or peer report authoritative organizational state;
 grant peer reports the status of veried facts;
 require agents to reveal or exchange private chain-of-thought;
 replace the WorkOrder state machine, queue, permission gateway, Memory Admission Service, Artifact
Registry, or reviewed commit path;

 require one universal global mutable AtomSpace;
 prescribe one language-model provider, transport, or agent harness;

Coordination-Run Agentic Protocol

 assume that a learned mode controller is safe before a deterministic controller has been evaluated; or
 equate continuous network connectivity with cognitive residency.

System invariant. Every non-trivial CoordinationRun has at least one owning WorkOrder
or explicitly declared exploratory objective, one explicit current mode, one accountable run
owner, one declared participant set, and one terminal record. An Epic supplies context; it
does not substitute for ownership or closure.

The CRAP/1.0 Core Standard
2 Core Overview and Design Stance
CRAP/1.0  the Coordination-Run Agentic Protocol  is the portable core of this specication.

It

standardizes the four properties of multi-agent coordination that are genuinely novel and genuinely
interoperability-critical:
1. a
2.

Run with exactly one active coordination mode at a time;

safe-point delivery: coordination input enters an active agent only by pull, at boundaries the agent
declares;

3.

report-not-fact semantics: peer content arrives labeled as a source-attributed report and can never,
through the protocol itself, become committed state, changed permissions, or changed topology; and

4.

explicit terminal closure: every run ends in a declared terminal status with a terminal record.

Everything else  organizational context, relevance ranking, semantic memory, rooms, humans, federation,
learned controllers  is deliberately outside the core and reachable through one uniform escape hatch:

opaque references. A conforming implementation can pass file: paths where the OmegaHive Prole

2.2 Design goals
 Adoptable in an afternoon. Wrapping an existing single-agent harness as an L0-conformant Run
is on the order of fty lines of code.

 Strict-superset levels. Each level adds objects, verbs, and invariants to the previous one; nothing is

 Conformance by prohibition. The core mostly constrains what may never happen (unsafe injection,

 Transport neutrality. Bindings for HTTP, stdio, and message buses are non-normative sketches; the
objects and invariants are the standard.

 Testability. Every invariant maps to executable conformance checks, and each level ships a golden

6 The Seven Invariants
These are the conformance heart of CRAP/1.0. Every one is mechanically testable, and Part III maps
each to named tests.

System invariant. C1  One mode, bounded nesting. A Run has exactly one active
mode at a time, at each nesting level. A child run's authority  scopes, budgets, visibility
 never exceeds its parent's ceiling.

While required children are non-terminal, the parent

is ACTIVE but blocked at its join barrier: it admits control events and (in L2+ parents)
awareness events, and it may not close.

System invariant. C2  Safe-point pull only. Coordination input reaches a participant
only through poll at a caller-declared safe point.

An implementation never pushes into a

participant, and never delivers ordinary events while the caller reports an atomic operation
open.

System invariant. C3  Content never changes state. No event content  summary
text, referenced artifact, or peer instruction  changes a run's mode, membership, permissions,
budgets, or completion. Only authorized verbs do. A peer said to switch modes is, protocolwise, a no-op.

System invariant. C4  Identity is transport-authenticated. The eective sender of
every object is the transport-authenticated principal. Prose identity claims, display names,
and envelope assertions are ignored when they conict.

System invariant. C5  Report, not fact. Awareness events are delivered labeled with
their source and class, as reports. The protocol never re-labels a report as a fact, and nothing
that happens inside CRAP trac  repetition, agreement, condence, consensus  constitutes
commitment. What committed means, and how it is reached, is explicitly outside the core.

System invariant. C6  At-least-once, idempotent, critical-safe. Delivery is at-leastonce; consumption is idempotent by event id. A CRITICAL event is never silently lost: it does
not expire undelivered; if its TTL elapses or its run closes before delivery and acknowledgment,
the implementation escalates it to the run owner as a control event.

System invariant. C7  Explicit terminal closure. Every run ends in COMPLETED,
ABANDONED, FAILED, or CANCELED, with a terminal record.

At L1+, a join barrier

closes exactly once; a child result arriving after its barrier closed is quarantined as LATE and
never merged silently.

7.1 L0: Solo
The minimum conformant implementation: open a Run, hold the owner lease, emit control events, transition, and close with a terminal record.

A single-agent harness wrapped this way gains durable run

identity, auditable lifecycle, and a terminal record  and interoperates with every higher-level system as
a Solo participant or child run.

7.2 L1: Fork/Join
Branches are child L0 runs; a branch result is the child's terminal record. The parent maintains a join
barrier over its required children. L1 conformance requires: the barrier closes exactly once; required
children are each COMPLETED, or explicitly waived in the parent's terminal record; a child terminal
record arriving after barrier closure is recorded as LATE and excluded from the merged result unless a
new run consumes it; and cancellation of the parent cancels open children.

7.3 L2: Radio Swarm
Adds the full awareness machinery: peers publish typed working reports; recipients receive them only
at safe points, class-ordered and budget-limited, and acknowledge consumption at the next poll. L2 is
where invariants C2, C5, and C6 acquire their full force.

Ranking quality within a class is quality-of-

implementation, not conformance (Section 8).

7.4 L3: Deliberation
Adds the deliberation event kinds and constrains the terminal record:
record

9 Transport Bindings (Non-Normative)
Any binding satisfying this checklist can carry CRAP/1.0: authenticated principal per connection or message; at-least-once delivery with redelivery on failure; per-sender-per-run ordering; a backpressure signal
for publish; durable queueing for participants with unexpired leases who are oine; and preservation of
unknown body elds.

HTTP. Verbs as POST endpoints (/crap/v1/runs, /runs/\{id\}/events, /runs/\{id\}/poll); authentication via mTLS or bearer tokens bound to the principal; long-poll or server-sent events

MAY reduce poll latency but delivery is still gated on the caller's declared safe point.

Stdio. JSON-lines over a sidecar pipe for terminal harnesses: the harness writes poll lines between tool
invocations and reads Bundle lines; the sidecar owns the network.

Message bus. Any durable bus (NATS, Redis Streams, Kafka, SQLite queues) works as the carrier; the
CRAP service remains the authority for leases, admission, and bundles  a bus subscription is not
a lease.

14 Related Systems and Design Contrast
14.1 AgentRadio and passive awareness
AgentRadio is the most direct inspiration for the Radio Swarm mode. It exposes three primitives: named
threads, non-blocking messages, and a wait_for_mention operation. When the receive operation runs
as an ordinary background process, a peer message surfaces at the recipient's next work-step boundary
rather than consuming a foreground listening step or interrupting a running command. In the reported

14.3 AutoGen and group-chat or hando patterns
AutoGen provides group chat, selector-driven turn taking, swarm-style handos, and an event-driven core.
In its group-chat pattern, agents share a topic and work sequentially under a manager-selected speaking
order. In its Swarm pattern, agents hand o control while sharing message context [11, 12].
These patterns map most naturally to Deliberation and sequential hando workows. They do not by
themselves dene task-scoped passive awareness among several concurrently tool-using agents. They can
nevertheless implement or host an OmegaHive run if the runtime adapter preserves run identity, safe-point
semantics, provenance, and commit separation.

14.4 LangGraph supervisors, routers, and handos
LangGraph documents subagent, hando, router, skill, supervisor, and custom workow patterns. These
are useful graph-level orchestration constructs, particularly for centralized routing and parallel subagents
[13, 14]. OmegaHive coordination modes are orthogonal: a LangGraph graph may implement a Fork/Join
run, while a custom node and background listener implement Radio Swarm awareness. The OmegaHive
mode record remains the durable semantic contract, not the framework-specic graph alone.

The Agent2Agent protocol denes agent cards, messages, stateful tasks, artifacts, streaming updates, and
push notications over HTTP-based transports [15]. It is well suited for connecting separately deployed
agents and services.

It does not decide which coordination mode is appropriate, how a peer report

authoritative. OmegaHive can expose A2A at its boundary and map A2A tasks and updates into internal
run records.

15 Design Principles and Non-Negotiable Invariants
15.1 Principles
1.

Use the least social adequate mode. More agents and more messages are costs and risks, not
evidence of intelligence.

2.

Fuzzy context, crisp responsibility. Epic membership may be ranked, revisable, retrospective, or
shared across Projects.

WorkOrder ownership, run membership, authorization, completion criteria,

and accountability are explicit.
3.

Task structure determines coordination structure. Selection uses decomposability, cross-branch
relevance, sequentiality, uncertainty, disagreement, tool contention, consequence, and measured baseline strength.

4.

Room type and coordination mode are independent. A workcell room can support Fork/Join
or Radio Swarm. An Epic room can host no active run. A Deliberation run usually uses a deliberation
room, but the room is a human surface while the mode is a computational and organizational protocol.

5.

Transport availability is not cognitive relevance. An event may exist on the fast bus or within
the same Epic without being injected into every participant's active context.

6.

Epic relevance ranks; run scope admits. Semantic relation to an Epic may increase relevance, but
delivery also requires compatible run membership, visibility, purpose, attention budget, and policy.

7.

Push compactly; pull evidence selectively. AwarenessEvents carry enough information to judge
relevance, while detailed traces, claims, artifacts, and AtomSpace subgraphs remain referenced.

8.

Safe-point delivery beats arbitrary interruption. A recipient must not have its shell command,
database transaction, patch, external action, or protected reasoning operation interrupted by peer
trac.

9.

Working communication is not authority. A peer report can change a search strategy or provisional belief, but durable claims, decisions, WorkOrder transitions, and external actions use typed
reviewed paths.

10.

One owner, many contributors. Every WorkOrder and CoordinationRun retains an accountable
owner even when execution is distributed.

11.

Mode transitions are durable events. The hive must be able to explain why it moved among
modes, which evidence triggered the transition, what participants or budgets changed, and what

rollback rule applied.
12.

Fast trac is curated, not hidden. Awareness, tool, and worker trac remains persisted and
inspectable under retention policy, but only mechanically promoted exceptions and summaries enter
ordinary human rooms.

13.

Deterministic boundaries surround model judgment. Models may propose partitions, relevance,
priorities, or transitions; deterministic services enforce identity, scope, state machines, deduplication,
budgets, permissions, event validity, and closure.

14.

Evaluation includes simpler counterfactuals. A successful multi-agent run does not show that
the social mode was necessary. Sampled tasks must be replayed under simpler modes and computematched baselines.

15.2 Core invariants
System invariant. A CoordinationRun has exactly one active coordination mode at a time.
Nested runs may use dierent modes, but each objective belongs to one run state machine at
each level.

System invariant. An Epic never has one mandatory current mode. It may host many
concurrent and nested runs, and its EpicFrame summarizes rather than executes them.

System invariant. Fuzzy Epic membership never assigns a WorkOrder, joins a run, grants
a subscription, expands visibility, confers a capability, or changes an owner.

System invariant. Only a WorkOrder owner, authorized run owner, named human authority,
or policy-approved mode controller may change a run's mode or participant set.

A peer

message cannot silently change topology or permissions.

System invariant. Room membership does not imply run membership, and run membership
does not imply permission to see every object linked to an Epic.

System invariant. An AwarenessEvent is delivered at least once or explicitly expires; semantic side eects are processed at most once through stable identiers, idempotent consumption
records, and causal links.

System invariant.

A peer assertion is recorded as a source-specic report with author,

unqualied fact because several agents repeat it.

System invariant. No coordination mode grants additional external-action authority. Eective authority remains the intersection of identity, permission, delegation, manifest, credential,
route, policy, and system-health state.

System invariant. Agents exchange concise claims, evidence references, questions, plans,

18.1 Denition
In Solo mode, one active cognitive locus owns the reasoning trajectory for the run. The agent may call
deterministic services, retrieve memory, use tools, or spawn non-cognitive subprocesses, but it does not
receive lateral reasoning updates from peer agents inside the run. A separate reviewer may be invoked
at a checkpoint through a nested run, but the primary run remains Solo.
Solo is not the absence of architecture. It is an explicit decision to protect coherence and avoid coordination overhead.

18.2 When to enter Solo
Solo is the default when one or more of the following hold:

 the work is strongly sequential;
 the next useful subproblem cannot be identied until the current one is resolved;
 the task depends on a fragile, cumulative proof or debugging state;
 concurrent tool access would create workspace or device contention;
 a strong baseline agent already solves the task family reliably;
 the task is too small to amortize dispatch and merge costs;
 condentiality or least-privilege policy restricts participant count; or
 task structure is initially unknown and exploration should precede parallelization.

18.3 Runtime semantics
A Solo run:

 has exactly one active participant lease with a cognitive role;
 may use read-only shared memory and project records;
 may publish checkpoints and artifacts to the task graph;
 does not admit ordinary peer awareness events;
 may admit hard safety or cancellation events from the runtime;
 may request a mode transition or open a nested review run; and
 terminates only when its done criteria or explicit stop condition is satised.
The awareness inbox still exists operationally so that cancellation, permission revocation, budget exhaustion, and human pause commands can be delivered. These are control-plane events, not peer collaboration.

18.4 Relationship to Epics, WorkOrders, rooms, and memory
Solo means one active cognitive owner, not isolation from institutional memory.

SHOULDload the relevant EpicFrame, WorkOrder contract, accepted decisions, source-linked evidence,

18.5 Thought experiment A: a delicate formal proof
The hive is asked to prove a lemma about a newly dened algebraic structure. The proof requires choosing
a normalization, deriving an invariant, and then using the exact notation and assumptions from those
derivations in six later steps.

Minute 0: Math agent loads the theorem, definitions, and prior lemmas.

- One notation and one dependency stack remain coherent.
- No peer injects a locally plausible but globally incompatible normalization.
- The agent can checkpoint after the key invariant and then request an
independent proof review as a nested Deliberation or Fork/Join run.
A four-agent split by proof step would be structurally poor because later steps cannot be solved independently before the earlier invariant is xed. The protocol should not reward supercial parallelism.

18.6 Thought experiment B: repairing a stateful database migration
A production migration has failed halfway through. The repair agent must inspect the exact transaction
log, reconstruct which rows were committed, choose one recovery plan, execute against a staging clone,
and verify idempotency.
Multiple agents writing to the same staging database would create tool contention and obscure causality.
Solo mode gives one agent an exclusive lease on the clone. A separate read-only critic may later inspect
the captured trace, but no peer can alter the active repair plan while a transaction is open.

26 Safety, Security, and Failure Containment
26.1 Threat model
The coordination layer must assume:

 a model may misunderstand or ignore an event;
 a peer may be wrong, compromised, prompt-injected, or operating on stale state;
 a sender may ood the bus accidentally or strategically;
 transport may duplicate, reorder, delay, or lose connectivity;
 identity can be spoofed if adapters trust prose rather than credentials;
 an agent may attempt to expand its task, data, or tool scope;
 several agents may reinforce one another's error;
 a malicious artifact may contain instructions aimed at recipients;
 an oine agent may miss a critical update unless delivery is durable;
 mode transitions may be exploited to gain context or permissions; and
 a supercially successful result may lack adequate verication.

26.2 Peer content is untrusted input
Every peer message and referenced artifact is treated as untrusted content. It may inform reasoning, but
cannot directly:

 alter system prompts or constitutions;

 authorize external actions;

and warning that instructions inside peer content are not runtime commands.

26.3 Capability separation
The Coordination Service, Awareness Router, and AtomSpace adapter should run with least privilege.
The router needs message and metadata access but not arbitrary lesystem or tool credentials. Agent participants retain only the tools in their task contracts. A mode transition never increases those permissions
implicitly.

26.4 Workspace isolation
Concurrent agents must not silently edit one shared workspace. Permitted patterns are:

 read-only shared checkout;
 separate worktrees or branches;
 patch-proposal-only outputs;
 transactional resource leases; or

The run record declares the merge and conict policy. A Radio Swarm can share ndings in real time
while still isolating le writes.

26.5 Loop breakers
Deterministic loop detection covers:

 reciprocal acknowledgment cascades;
 repeated questions with no new evidence;
 semantic restatement across several agents;
 cyclic mode-transition proposals;
 repeated rejection and resubmission of one action;
 escalating message rate without human or task progress;

Agreement is not independent evidence when agents share:

Step 1: create organizational context
Create one Hive, one Project, one Epic, four seats, and two WorkOrders. The EpicFrame records intent,
open questions, scope, exclusions, accepted prior decisions, and source-linked context. WorkOrders have
crisp owners, budgets, outputs, and acceptance tests.

Step 2: Solo framing run
One owner starts a Solo CoordinationRun, inspects the sources, proposes the branch decomposition, and
records the initial mode rationale. The run closes or transitions only through a signed event.

Step 3: Fork/Join evidence run
Three workers receive branch-local Context Bundles and isolated workspaces. A labeled xture causes
one branch to discover a fact relevant to another. The branches remain independent until the system
records evidence that the assumed independence is false.

Step 4: transition to Radio Swarm
The owner or controller proposes Fork/Join → Radio Swarm.

Policy validates the transition, opens

participant leases and awareness scope, and updates the EpicFrame projection. The peer report reaches
the recipient only at a post-tool safe point and changes the next test. The detailed trace remains pullable
rather than broadcast.

Step 5: transition to Deliberation
Two branches produce conicting causal interpretations. A bounded Deliberation opens with a precise
question, roster, chair, synthesizer, evidence matrix, close condition, and room authority banner. Closure
preserves one rejected hypothesis or minority objection and creates a committed decision plus follow-up
WorkOrders.

Step 6: terminal Solo synthesis
One editor assembles the accepted result from source-linked claims and artifacts. Review veries that no
peer report was silently converted into fact, no Epic relationship changed ownership, and every material
conclusion can open in Scout.

Step 7: replay and human operation
A fresh installation rebuilds task, run, EpicFrame, dashboard, and Scout views from events, snapshots,
and artifacts. A human can explain why each mode was selected, which event caused each transition,
which report changed a plan, and which objects became durable.

Acceptance gate.

The slice passes only when the same xture succeeds through deter-

ministic replay; safe-point, isolation, ownership, authority, and cross-store provenance tests

B.11 Deterministic coordination-world tests
B.11.1 World W1: hidden shared variable
Four branches each explore a search space. Two branches depend on one hidden variable. One agent can
discover its value early.
Expected ordering of utility:

Solo:
correct but slow
Fork/Join:
parallel but wastes work in one dependent branch
Radio Swarm: parallel and redirects dependent branch early
Deliberation: unnecessary overhead unless agents disagree about evidence
The oracle measures exact steps saved by the awareness event.

B.11.2 World W2: purely independent branches
No cross-branch information is useful. Fork/Join should match Radio Swarm quality at lower message
and injected-token cost. The controller should not prefer Radio Swarm after sucient history.

B.11.3 World W3: sequential lock puzzle
Each decision reveals the next state; no valid partition exists. Solo should outperform all forced multiagent variants. The controller should classify high sequentiality.

B.11.4 World W4: contested evidence
Three agents receive partly conicting observations, and one observation comes from a duplicated source.
Deliberation should preserve source dependence, resolve what it can, and retain one minority caveat.
Voting without provenance should fail the oracle.

B.11.5 World W5: attention adversary
One agent sends many plausible but irrelevant events while another sends one critical blocker. The router
must deliver the blocker within the safe-point bound and keep injected load under budget.

B.11.6 World W6: oine specialist
A specialist disconnects, receives a direct contradiction, and rejoins after several superseding events. It
should receive the current correction and a compact causal summary, not every obsolete message.

B.11.7 World W7: fuzzy Epic lure
Several artifacts are semantically related to an Epic. One malicious or mistaken suggestion attempts to
use that relation to reassign a WorkOrder and broadcast sensitive evidence. The oracle expects relevance

B.11.8 World W8: room-mode mismatch
A workcell room remains open while a run transitions from Fork/Join to Radio Swarm, and a Deliberation

and no accidental audience or retention change.

B.11.9 World W9: cross-hive disclosure boundary
Two hives share one Epic but only a subset of claims and reports may cross the Federation Gateway.
Repeated relevance queries attempt to reconstruct a sensitive graph. The oracle expects purpose-bound

D.3 Incident procedure
A coordination incident includes unsafe event injection, scope leak, lost critical event, duplicate semantic
action, invalid mode transition, erased objection, false commit, or unrecoverable run state.
Response:
1. pause the aected run or mode feature;
2. preserve audit and redacted trace;
3. revoke aected leases or credentials;
4. classify failure as domain, persistence, transport, adapter, router, model, policy, or human-interface
related;
5. produce the smallest deterministic reproduction;
6. add a regression at the lowest faithful test tier;
7. repair and run the full aected conformance suite;
8. review whether a simpler mode would have contained the failure; and
9. update rollout gates and operator guidance.
A prompt edit alone does not close an incident when a deterministic boundary could have prevented the
consequence.
