 1

Introduction and Vision

Operating systems have always encoded a theory of who operates them. The terminal assumed
an expert; the desktop metaphor assumed an office worker; the smartphone assumed a consumer.
Each generation moved the interface closer to human intention and pushed mechanism further
below the surface. Omega Linux takes the next step: the primary operator of the machine is a
cognitive system — a hive of cooperating OmegaClaw agents — and the human interacts with
the machine at the level of goals, questions, and approvals rather than commands, dialogs, and
configuration files.
Concretely, Omega Linux is an existing, proven Linux base, modified so that:
 A resident multi-agent hive runs as a set of system services, continuously perceiving the
machine through its logs, event buses, and (when appropriate) its display surfaces.
 The hive maintains a persistent knowledge-graph world model of the machine and its user
in a Hyperon AtomSpace, over which it can perform genuine inference, not merely retrieval.
 All mutations of system state flow through a deterministic, typed action broker with
graduated confirmation policies, never through raw shell access.
 The default login session is a hive surface — conversation, a live run board, and pendingapproval diffs — with the terminal and traditional applications one keystroke away.
 The entire system configuration is declarative and transactional, so every hive-initiated
change is a reviewable diff and every generation of the system is rollbackable.

Two properties distinguish this from the “AI PC” copilots now being bolted onto commercial
operating systems. First, Omega Linux is resident and stateful : the hive lives on the machine,
accumulates a world model over months and years, and acts with continuity, rather than being a
stateless assistant invoked per keystroke. Second, it is open and auditable end to end : the agents,
the broker, the policies, the world model, and (in the default configuration) the underlying
language models are all inspectable and modifiable by the owner of the machine. The large
platform vendors can imitate the first property only partially and the second not at all.
The vision is deliberately dual-purpose. As a product line, Omega Linux addresses concrete,
monetizable pain across server fleets, small-business infrastructure, education, accessibility,
robotics, and embedded devices. As a research artifact, it is a forcing function and a public
demonstration: a hive that competently operates real machines, including the machines it itself
runs on, is a visible, verifiable step in the proto-AGI program — and its architecture (typed
actuation, taint-aware world models, guardian oversight, transactional reversibility) is a working
example of how powerful agentic AI can be deployed accountably.

2

Product Concept

2.1

What Omega Linux Is

Omega Linux is delivered in three forms, in order of maturity:

3

 1. The Omega Layer (flake). A set of NixOS modules that any user can add to an existing
NixOS machine, installing the hive services, the action broker, the AtomSpace world model,
and the hive session. This is the open-source core and the community on-ramp.
2. Omega Linux (distribution). A branded, installable distribution (ISO and preinstalled
images) in which the hive session is the default target and the system is configured for one
of the product profiles below.
3. Omega Device OS (embedded/robotics profile). A slimmed, cross-compiled variant
for robots and embedded devices, running a thin edge agent on constrained hardware with
an uplink to a supervising hive, or a fuller onboard hive on capable edge silicon.

2.2

Product Profiles

A single core platform supports several profiles that differ in guardian policy, actuation defaults,
UX, and model placement, in the spirit of the OmegaClaw Access / OmegaClaw Lab split:
Omega Fleet. Server profile. No graphical session; the hive is reachable via chat endpoints
(Slack, SSH-attached TUI, web run board). Conservative actuation defaults: all diffs
reviewed by a human or a designated senior Guardian until autonomy is earned per-site.
Aimed at ops teams.
Omega Desk. Enthusiast / developer desktop. Hive session as default, liberal actuation for
user-space verbs, conservative for system verbs. Community supported.
Omega Learn. Education profile. Locked-down actuation, multi-user awareness, classroom
administration by the hive, and — distinctively — pedagogical transparency mode: the
run board, agent deliberations, guardian policies, and world model are surfaced as firstclass curriculum objects for AI-literacy teaching.
Omega Access. Disability-first profile, the desktop sibling of OmegaClaw Access: fully conversational operation, aggressive proactive assistance, simplified confirmation surfaces, coordinated with the Android Access work as one accessibility program spanning phone and
desktop.
Omega Home / Omega SMB. Appliance profile for family and small-business servers (files,
backup, media, light services), administered entirely conversationally, sold through and
alongside managed service providers.
Omega Body. Robotics profile developed with the Mindchildren project: the perception layer
ingests robot sensors, the action broker drives actuators under a safety-governor Guardian,
and cognition is split between onboard reflexes and hive-level deliberation.

2.3

What Omega Linux Is Not

 It is not a replacement for the terminal or for applications. Both remain fully installed,
supported, and one keystroke away. Omega Linux demotes them from default to fallback ;
it does not remove them.

4

  It is not a cloud assistant with local hooks. The hive is resident; the default configuration
runs on open-weights models locally or on the owner’s own server, with frontier API calls
as an optional accelerant.
 It is not an autonomy maximalist system. The architecture is built around graduated,
earned autonomy, with review surfaces and reversibility as the core product experience,
not as compliance afterthoughts.

3

Use Cases

The use cases split into two families with complementary value propositions: server-oriented
cases monetize reduced labor (autonomy with accountability), and retail-oriented cases monetize
reduced expertise (capability without administration). Robotics and embedded form a third
family that inherits from both.

3.1
3.1.1

Server-Oriented Use Cases
Self-Operating Fleets

Each server runs a hive (or a thin agent reporting to a central hive) that handles patching,
service health, log triage, capacity planning, and incident response, proposing changes as diffs
to the declarative system configuration. The pitch is not “no operations staff” but a change
in leverage: one operator supervises hundreds of machines by reviewing diffs and run boards
instead of opening shells. The immutable, transactional base is what makes this credible where
generic “AI SRE” offerings hand-wave: agent fallibility is converted from “corrupted system”
into “rejected or reverted diff.”
3.1.2

Incident Response and Forensics

Because the hive has been continuously watching the journal, event bus, and kernel-level probes,
it holds the causal history of an incident in its world model before a human is paged. It can
run a structured deliberation over hypotheses, correlate with incidents months old (the world
model persists), and present a human with a diagnosis and a proposed, reviewable remediation.
Time-to-diagnosis, not automation of the fix, is the initially marketable win.
3.1.3

Resident Security Posture

A hive that lives on the box performs continuous anomaly detection, tracks the provenance of
what touched what, and can quarantine through broker verbs rather than merely alert. This
is the Tyrian4 / Omega Purple overlap: an agentic security office that ships as the operating
system is differentiated against agentless scanners, and the two products reinforce each other
commercially (fleets that buy one adopt the other).
3.1.4

Self-Provisioning Research Compute

GPU servers and ephemeral cloud nodes (e.g. RunPod-class instances) that prepare themselves
for whatever experiment a dispatching agent requires, and that diagnose and repair their own
environments when jobs fail. This case is immediately consumed internally by OmegaHive1 and

5

 the agent-run experimental programs, and it closes the recursive loop: infrastructure for the
proto-AGI hive, operated by the hive.
3.1.5

The Dark Server

The long-horizon server concept: machines with no routine human login path at all. The hive
endpoint is the administrative interface; terminal access is a break-glass procedure. This inverts
today’s default (humans in, agents bolted on) and is arguably the safer end state, since standing
human remote access is itself a major attack surface.

3.2
3.2.1

Retail-Oriented Use Cases
Education (Lead Retail Wedge)

Omega Learn addresses two distinct education needs at once:
 The machine as curriculum object. Contemporary AI-literacy programs teach students to prompt a black box. Omega Linux is the AI you can open up: students inspect
the run board, read the Guardian’s policies, watch a multi-agent deliberation, query the
AtomSpace, and edit an agent’s verb permissions to see what changes. This teaches how
agentic AI actually works, hands-on, on hardware the school owns — a pedagogical proposition no bundled copilot can match, and one that converts the platform’s auditability
from a security feature into the product itself.
 The machine as administrable classroom fleet. School computer labs on inexpensive
hardware, self-maintaining, centrally supervised by a district-level hive, with near-zero
demands on scarce school IT staff — the Chromebook precedent shows that institutions
will adopt a locked-down Linux at scale when the administration burden approaches zero.

The education wedge proceeds on three clocks: university CS and AI departments first (fast
adoption, no procurement friction, and the resulting research community follows the ROS playbook in which academic ubiquity later pulls industry along); AI-literacy grant programs second
(foundation and government funding for AI education is currently abundant, and funders favor
open source, accessibility, and hardware sovereignty); K-12 procurement third (slow, but large).
There is additionally a strong developing-world fit — low-cost hardware, local open-weights
models, and a machine that administers itself are exactly what environments with scarce IT capacity and connectivity need — continuous with the ecosystem’s long-standing education work
in Ethiopia and elsewhere. Crucially, the Mindchildren robotics project’s own initial focus is
the education market, so the education and robotics wedges are one coordinated motion (Section 3.3).
3.2.2

Accessibility

Omega Access serves users who are functionally locked out of desktop computing: elderly users,
non-technical users, and users with disabilities. A laptop one talks to — which installs software,
repairs connectivity, finds documents, and never presents a configuration dialog — is a different
product category, not a better Linux. The channel is institutional (disability organizations,
aging-in-place programs, accessibility procurement) rather than consumer retail; margins are

6

 modest but the market is uncontested, mission-central, and grant-fundable, and it anchors the
human-impact narrative of the whole product line.
3.2.3

Small-Business and Family Servers

A NAS-class appliance in a home or a five-person business runs backup, shared files, media, and
light services, administered entirely conversationally. The price anchor is the managed-serviceprovider contract it partially replaces; the initial channel is through MSPs, as a tool that lets
one technician serve several times the clients, so that the eventual disintermediation is preceded
by a period in which MSPs are the distribution.
3.2.4

Enthusiast and Developer Desktops

For users who can administer machines but prefer not to spend weekends doing so: the machine
gardens itself — dependency rot, backup discipline, dotfile drift, disk hygiene — with everything
reviewable as diffs. The Nix community is the beachhead (declarative configuration is already
their religion, and a conversational layer over Nix has standalone value given Nix’s learning
curve); the broader enthusiast world follows on novelty and status (a hive session that looks like
nothing else propagates on screenshots alone). This segment is addressed in parallel from the
start, because it is nearly free: the enthusiast product is the open-source flake itself, community
supported, and it functions as the funnel into fleet deals via the classic developer-champion
motion.
3.2.5

Personal Knowledge Infrastructure

Because the hive perceives the user’s activity and maintains a persistent world model, the
machine becomes a genuine second memory: retrieval by meaning and episode (“the paper I
skimmed in March about erasure codes”), resumption of abandoned threads, proactive surfacing.
Every AI-PC vendor gestures at this; a resident hive with a persistent AtomSpace can actually
do it. This is the largest long-term prize and the most contested; it is treated as an emergent
capability of the platform rather than a launch product.

3.3
3.3.1

Robotics and Embedded
Robotics with Mindchildren

A robot needs precisely the stack Omega Linux provides: a perception layer feeding a world
model, a typed action broker (now driving actuators, with the Guardian as safety governor —
a framing regulators will recognize and approve of), and a reflex-versus-deliberation split across
edge and hive that transplants the OmegaClaw Android edge/personal-server pattern onto a
robot body. The robotics profile is therefore a port, not a new product.
The collaboration with Mindchildren is doubly synergistic because Mindchildren’s own initial
market focus is education. Education robots running Omega Body, deployed into classrooms
alongside Omega Learn machines and supervised by the same school hive, constitute a single
integrated offering: the classroom’s computers and its robots are one transparent, inspectable
cognitive ecosystem, and the robots themselves are curriculum objects in the same pedagogicaltransparency sense. Mindchildren thus serves simultaneously as reference customer, co-developer
of the robotics profile, and co-marketer in the education channel.
7

 3.3.2

Embedded Systems, Approached Correctly

The embedded market is large but conservative, certification-bound, and hostile to new operating
systems; one does not pitch it a distribution. Robotics is the correct entry because it is the one
embedded segment that is culturally permissive: research and consumer robots ship on generalpurpose Linux today and tolerate novelty. The product embedded buyers are eventually sold —
arriving from robotics with credibility — is not an OS but fleet operations for unattended devices:
nobody wants to open shells on five thousand kiosks or eight hundred warehouse robots. A thin
hive agent per device reporting to a supervising hive, with diff-reviewed over-the-air updates on
an immutable base, is the fleet-ops product wearing embedded clothes. Robotics is the foot in
the door; device fleet management is the room.

4

Requirements

4.1

Functional Requirements

F1. The system SHALL run a resident hive of named agents as supervised system services,
with configurable seat rosters per profile.
F2. The hive SHALL perceive system state through the journal, D-Bus, filesystem notification, kernel-level probes (eBPF), and, with explicit per-session consent, display capture
via desktop portals.
F3. The hive SHALL maintain a persistent AtomSpace world model of system state, configuration, provenance, user preferences and habits, and task history, queryable by all
agents and (in transparency modes) by the user.
F4. All mutations of system state SHALL flow through a typed action broker exposing a
versioned verb vocabulary (package management, configuration editing, service management, file operations, application control, network operations; actuator verbs in the
robotics profile).
F5. The broker SHALL enforce an actuation ladder per verb class and per provenance taint:
auto-execute, notify, confirm, strong-confirm (passphrase or second factor), and forbidden.
F6. Every system-level change SHALL be expressible as a reviewable diff against declarative
configuration, applied transactionally, with one-step rollback to any recent generation.
F7. The default session SHALL present conversation, a live run board of coordination runs,
and pending approvals; the terminal and conventional applications SHALL remain installed and reachable within one action.
F8. Multi-step work SHALL be organized as CRAP/1.0 coordination runs (Solo, Fork/Join,
Radio Swarm, Deliberation), inspectable on the run board and exportable for audit.
F9. Agents SHALL be able to request sandboxed exploratory shells (namespace-isolated, no
mutation of real state) distinct from broker actuation.

8

 F10. The system SHALL operate with full core functionality on local open-weights models,
with remote frontier models as an optional, per-verb-class configurable accelerant.
F11. The hive SHALL support delegation hierarchies: a device-level hive or thin agent MAY
report to a site-level or fleet-level hive, with policy flowing down and telemetry and
proposals flowing up.
F12. Education profile: the system SHALL expose pedagogical transparency mode, including
read access to runs, deliberations, guardian policy, and world model, and a safe policyediting sandbox for students.
F13. Access profile: the system SHALL be fully operable by conversation (text and voice), with
proactive assistance and simplified confirmation surfaces meeting relevant accessibility
standards.
F14. Robotics profile: actuator verbs SHALL be governed by a safety-governor Guardian with
deterministic interlocks that do not depend on model inference for enforcement.

4.2

Non-Functional Requirements

N1. Reversibility. Any hive-initiated system change is undoable in one step; the machine
is never more than one command from its previous known-good generation.
N2. Ambient efficiency. Continuous perception and world-model maintenance run within
strict budgets (target: under 5% of one core and a bounded memory envelope on desktop;
profile-specific budgets for embedded), with the full hive waking on request or anomaly
rather than polling expensively.
N3. Latency. Routine conversational interactions respond within interactive latency on local
models; the machine must never feel haunted or sluggish because of the hive.
N4. Offline operation. Core operation, including conversational control and local verbs,
functions with no network connectivity.
N5. Cost transparency. When remote models are enabled, projected and actual spend are
visible and capped per period.
N6. Auditability. Every actuation is logged with the initiating run, the evidence context,
the taint profile, and the approving principal; logs are tamper-evident.
N7. Portability. x86-64 and ARM64 from day one; cross-compilation to embedded targets
in the device profile.
N8. Graceful degradation. Failure of any hive component leaves a conventional, fully
functional Linux system.

4.3

Security Requirements (Summary)

Security requirements are elaborated with the trust model in Section 6; in brief: no agent ever
holds raw root; all actuation is broker-mediated and policy-checked; content-derived context is
taint-tracked from perception through to actuation decisions; guardian review is mandatory for
9

 runs touching tainted context above a threshold; the guardian runs a different model family
than worker agents; and the immutable base plus verb whitelisting bound the blast radius of
any compromise of a worker agent.

5

Architecture

5.1

Base Distribution: Declarative and Immutable

The single most consequential design decision is the base. Omega Linux builds on NixOS (with
an ostree-based immutable such as Fedora Silverblue as a secondary target for the appliance
profiles), for four reasons:
1. Agent legibility. The entire system configuration is a text artifact. Agents propose
changes as diffs to configuration, not as imperative command sequences whose effects no
one can predict.
2. Transactionality. Changes are atomic and produce numbered generations; a bad decision
is one rollback from undone. This converts agent fallibility from “corrupted system” to
“reverted diff,” which is the tolerable failure mode on which the entire trust story rests.
3. Reviewability. A diff is the natural unit of human oversight and of guardian oversight; the
approval surface of the whole product is the configuration diff plus the run that produced
it.
4. Reproducibility. Fleet and classroom deployments are declaratively specified and bitreproducible, which is what makes supervising hundreds of machines from one board sane.
A hive driving a mutable package manager would be a liability; a hive editing a Nix flake is a
transactional database client.

5.2
5.2.1

Layered Design
Layer 1: Perception

Agents subscribe to the machine’s native sensorium: the systemd journal, D-Bus signals, inotify/fanotify watches on relevant trees, eBPF probes for process and network events, hardware
telemetry, and — only with explicit consent, per session — Wayland screencast portals when visual grounding is required. On robots, this layer additionally ingests sensor streams through the
same event fabric. Linux is a far better substrate for machine perception than mobile platforms:
the operating system is introspectable by design, and no accessibility-service workarounds are
needed.
5.2.2

Layer 2: World Model (System AtomSpace)

A Jetta/Hyperon AtomSpace holds the machine as a knowledge graph: installed packages and
their provenance; configuration atoms mirroring the declarative config; running services and
their dependency structure; file and project semantics; user preferences, habits, and history;
incident and task episodes; and, critically, taint annotations recording which atoms derive from
untrusted content. The hive reasons over this model rather than re-parsing the filesystem per

10

 query. PLN inference over the world model is where the architecture earns its keep beyond a
bare LLM loop: causal and probabilistic structure across episodes (“this class of configuration
change has historically correlated with that class of failure”) is queryable knowledge, not vibes.
The world model also persists across model upgrades: the machine’s accumulated self-knowledge
is an asset independent of which LLM is currently seated.
5.2.3

Layer 3: Action Broker

The deterministic heart of the trust model, directly descended from the on-device action broker
in the OmegaClaw Android design. Agents never obtain a raw shell against real state. They call
typed verbs — install/remove package, edit configuration section, manage service, file operations,
launch and control applications, network operations, and (Omega Body) actuator commands —
against a broker daemon that:
 validates the verb and arguments against a versioned schema;
 consults policy: verb class, profile, principal, and the taint profile of the evidence context
behind the request;
 routes the action up the actuation ladder (auto / notify / confirm / strong-confirm /
forbidden) accordingly;
 executes through least-privilege mechanisms (polkit-mediated helpers, systemd transient
units, configuration-diff application), never through a general shell;
 logs the actuation with full provenance.

For exploration, agents may request sandboxed shells (bubblewrap or systemd-nspawn, no access
to real mutable state); anything they learn there becomes a proposal through the broker. In
the robotics profile, a deterministic safety interlock layer sits between broker and actuators and
does not depend on any model inference for enforcement.
5.2.4

Layer 4: Hive Fabric

The existing OmegaHive stack transplants directly: a NATS/Redis message bus; named agents
as supervised systemd services; Kanboard-class task state; Scout inspection; and CRAP/1.0
coordination runs as the unit of multi-step work. Illustratively: “set up a CUDA environment
for this repository” is a Fork/Join run; “why is the fan screaming” is a Solo diagnostic; “redesign
my backup strategy” is a Deliberation. The default desktop seat roster follows the five-seat
pattern of the Android design — Companion (user-facing voice), Executive (task ownership
and delegation), Systems Specialist (deep OS work), Memory Steward (world-model hygiene),
Guardian (policy, safety, and review) — with the Companion dropped and the Executive exposed
over chat endpoints in the Fleet profile. Delegation hierarchies connect device hives to site and
fleet hives using the same protocol, which is what makes classrooms, businesses, and robot fleets
one architecture rather than three.
5.2.5

Layer 5: Session and User Experience

The distribution’s flagship move: the default login target is a hive surface, not a desktop. A
Wayland session presents three primary panes — conversation, the live run board, and pending11

 approval diffs — with conventional applications and a terminal one keystroke away and fully
first-class. On servers, the “session” is the Executive’s chat endpoint plus the run board as a
web page. In Omega Learn’s transparency mode, the session additionally exposes deliberation
viewers, policy browsers, and the world-model inspector as teaching surfaces.

5.3

Model Placement

Model placement is hybrid and profile-dependent, with a strong bias toward local open weights:
 A local model (open-weights, Kimi-class or successor) handles ambient perception triage,
journaling, world-model maintenance, routine conversation, and low-stakes verbs. This
keeps the machine functional offline, keeps always-on costs sane, and keeps student and
household data on-premises.
 Frontier API models are an optional accelerant for hard runs, gated per verb class and per
profile, with visible spend caps.
 The Guardian runs a different model family than worker agents, so a single model’s failure
modes or a single-model jailbreak cannot simultaneously subvert workers and reviewer.

The education and robotics wedges make local open-weights operation the critical path rather
than a cost optimization: schools cannot ship student activity to third-party APIs, and robots
cannot block on network round trips. This is the longest-lead technical risk in the program and
is resourced accordingly.

5.4

Hardware Tiers

Tier A (workstation/server). Full hive, local model of substantial size, complete world model.
x86-64/ARM64 with GPU or capable NPU.
Tier B (capable edge). Robot main computers and premium edge boxes: full broker and
safety layer, reduced seat roster, compact local model, world-model synchronization with
a supervising hive.
Tier C (constrained embedded). Thin agent only: perception forwarding, broker with a
minimal verb set, deterministic interlocks; all cognition at the supervising hive. This tier
is what the embedded fleet-ops product ships on.

6

Security and Trust Model

6.1

Threat Model

The threat model is dominated by one fact: a desktop or fleet hive reads arbitrary files, mail,
web content, and logs, and holds real actuation power. Every document is therefore a potential
adversarial input, and prompt injection is a more severe problem here than in any chat product.
Secondary threats include compromise of a worker agent or its model, malicious or compromised
verb-pack and policy-pack extensions, confirmation-surface attacks (including audio injection in
voice-operated profiles), and classic supply-chain attacks on the distribution itself.

12

 6.2

Defenses

1. Typed-verb bottleneck. No raw shells against real state; the broker’s verb schema is
the total actuation surface, and it is small, versioned, and audited.
2. Taint tracking. Content-derived atoms carry provenance from perception onward; actuation policy weights confirmation requirements by the taint profile of the evidence behind a
request. A run whose context includes yesterday’s downloaded PDF cannot silently reach
strong verbs.
3. Guardian review. Runs touching tainted context above threshold, and all strong-verb
actuations, require Guardian sign-off; the Guardian’s model diversity prevents commonmode subversion.
4. Immutable base and reversibility. The blast radius of any successful manipulation is
bounded by the transactional configuration model; recovery is a rollback, and the tamperevident actuation log supports forensics.
5. Sandboxed exploration. Agent curiosity is channeled into namespaced sandboxes with
no path to real state except broker proposals.
6. Confirmation-surface hardening. Strong confirmations use channels that ambient
content cannot actuate (physical keypress, passphrase, second factor), with redaction of
sensitive tokens (e.g. one-time codes) from agent-visible perception, carrying over the corresponding Android-design mitigations.
7. Signed extension ecosystem. Verb packs and policy packs are signed and reviewed;
the marketplace (when it arrives) inherits the review pipeline.

6.3

Relationship to Tyrian4 / Omega Purple

The distribution and the agentic security office are mutually reinforcing products: Omega Linux
ships with a resident security posture that Tyrian4 extends into a full monitored offering, while
Tyrian4 engagements create fleets predisposed to adopt Omega Fleet. A published third-party
security assessment of the broker and taint architecture is planned as a marketing asset, on the
principle that in this category the brakes are the product: the trust architecture is led with in
every sales conversation, because it is simultaneously the chief objection and, well executed, the
chief differentiator.

7

Go-to-Market Strategy

7.1

Strategic Principles

1. Credibility first, revenue second. “AI-run operating system” triggers maximal excitement and maximal distrust, and the first-paying audience (operations) is the most
skeptical audience in software. Trust is built with public evidence, not marketing.
2. Open source does the trust-building. The core is free and open (permissive license);
the communities that gate the buyers (Nix, SRE, robotics, education research) are courted
with real engineering presence, not developer marketing.
13

 3. Sell the brakes. Lead with reviewability, reversibility, taint-aware policy, and the
Guardian. Autonomy is earned per customer by track record, which is simultaneously
correct safety posture and correct sales motion.
4. Prefer standard-setting to incumbent-fighting. Each chosen wedge (Nix enthusiasts, education, robotics-into-embedded, crypto-infrastructure fleets) is a market where a
standard can be set before the platform vendors arrive, rather than a market where they
must be displaced.
5. One platform, entity-carried verticals. A single core team ships the flake, broker, and
profiles, and says no to vertical requests; each vertical is owned by an entity that already
exists and already wants it. This is what makes parallelism real rather than aspirational
for a small organization.
6. The GTM is also the research narrative. Public dogfooding and postmortems double
as proto-AGI program communication; the evidence base appreciates regardless of which
revenue line wins.

7.2

Parallel Tracks and Phasing

The motion is organized as parallel tracks on staggered clocks rather than a single sequential
funnel. Approximate phasing:
7.2.1

Phase 0 (months 0–6): Dogfood in Public

Run the Omega Layer on internal infrastructure: OmegaHive1 servers, RunPod and GPU nodes,
team laptops. Narrate it continuously — blog posts, workshop talks, incident postmortems with
public diffs. The deliverable of this phase is an evidence base, not users: months of visible, verifiable operation are what make every later conversation possible. The self-provisioning
research-compute case pays for itself internally during this phase.
7.2.2

Track 1 (months 3 onward): Enthusiast / Open-Source Land Grab

Ship the flake publicly under a permissive license, targeted first at the Nix community — small,
but exactly the right beachhead: declaratively minded, operationally influential, and immediately served by the standalone value of conversational Nix. Explicitly community-supported
(no SLA), so it never consumes commercial bandwidth. As the hive session matures, widen to
the broader enthusiast world, where a session that looks like nothing else propagates on novelty
alone. Success metrics: adoption, contributors, and mindshare in the venues that ops decisionmakers read. This track runs in parallel from the start; its cost is community management, and
its yield is the contributor moat (verb packs, policy packs, hardware quirk knowledge) and the
developer-champion funnel into fleet sales.
7.2.3

Track 2 (months 6 onward): Education, with Mindchildren

The lead retail wedge, run as one coordinated motion with the Mindchildren robotics project,
whose initial market focus is likewise education:

14

  Universities first. Omega Learn plus Omega Body as the platform for teaching and researching agentic systems; course materials, departmental pilots, and the AGI-conferenceadjacent research community as the springboard. The explicit model is ROS: academic
ubiquity first, industry pull later.
 Grant-funded AI-literacy programs second. Pedagogical transparency mode is the
differentiated offering; open source, accessibility, low-cost hardware, and data sovereignty
(local models; no student data leaving the building) align with funder criteria. Classroom
robots and classroom machines are one inspectable ecosystem and one grant application.
 K-12 procurement third. The Chromebook-precedent play: locked-down, cheap, selfadministering fleets supervised by a district hive, entering once the grant-program deployments have produced references.
 Developing-world deployments as a continuing thread through partner organizations,
where self-administration and offline local models are decisive advantages.

7.2.4

Track 3 (months 9–24): Fleet Operations Revenue

The primary commercial engine. Three to five design-partner pilots at meaningful fees (low six
figures) with organizations running 50–500 Linux machines and understaffed operations. Ideal
early segments: crypto and Web3 infrastructure operators (validator and node fleets — culturally aligned, ASI-Alliance-adjacent, high pain, novelty tolerant), GPU cloud and inference
startups, and research computing groups. Pilot structure: full human-review mode for months;
the product being sold is the run board and diff-review workflow, with autonomy expanded per
customer as track record accumulates. Post-pilot pricing: per-node-per-month subscription anchored against the fully loaded cost of operations headcount (one supervisor per several hundred
machines, versus one per twenty).
7.2.5

Track 4 (months 12 onward): Appliances and Access

 Omega Home / SMB as appliance or supported install on NAS-class hardware, priced
against MSP contracts and initially channeled through MSPs as a leverage tool.
 Omega Access through institutional and grant channels (disability organizations, agingin-place programs, accessibility procurement), coordinated with OmegaClaw Android Access as a single cross-device accessibility program.

7.2.6

Track 5 (months 18 onward): Robotics-to-Embedded Expansion

With Mindchildren deployments as the reference, extend Omega Body toward research and
commercial robotics generally, then pivot the offering for the broader embedded market into
device fleet management: Tier-C thin agents, supervising hives, diff-reviewed OTA on immutable
bases, sold to operators of kiosks, industrial edge boxes, and robot fleets. Embedded is never
pitched a new OS; it is pitched relief from operating unattended devices, arriving from robotics
with credibility.

15

 7.3

Positioning

Against the platform vendors’ operating-system copilots, Omega Linux occupies three positions
they structurally cannot:
1. Sovereignty. Runs on the owner’s hardware, on open weights, with data staying home
— the decentralized-AI thesis made concrete in a consumer-visible artifact, and a flagship
for the ASI Alliance ecosystem.
2. Auditability. Open agents, open broker, open policies, inspectable world model: “the AI
OS you can audit” and, in education, “the AI you can open up.”
3. Residency. A persistent, stateful cognitive system with a world model that compounds
over years, versus a stateless assistant.

7.4

Ecosystem and Token Layer

A decentralized layer is architecturally natural — hives sourcing specialist skills, inference, and
knowledge services from ASI ecosystem providers; a signed marketplace for verb packs, policy
packs, and seat personas — but it is deliberately excluded from the core pitch in Tracks 1–3,
because operations and education buyers are allergic to token mechanics. Ecosystem integration is introduced as an expansion story once the product has standalone credibility, at which
point Omega Linux endpoints become the most natural mass client surface the decentralized-AI
ecosystem has yet had.

7.5

Organization and Entity Mapping

 Core platform team (small): flake, broker, world model, session, profiles. Owns the
roadmap; declines vertical-specific work.
 BGI Labs (commercial): Omega Fleet pilots and subscriptions; later Home/SMB;
coordination with Tyrian4 / Omega Purple as the security layer and cross-sell.
 Foundation / non-profit side: Omega Learn and Omega Access; grant channels; opensource stewardship; developing-world programs.
 Mindchildren: Omega Body co-development; education-robotics reference deployments;
robotics channel.
 Community: Omega Desk; verb and policy pack ecosystem.
 Key early hire: not sales — a developer-relations and operations-credibility figure who
is visibly of the target tribe (known in Nix or SRE circles); their first year of talks, docs,
and postmortems is the Phase 0–1 GTM. The OmegaClaw/Hive product manager role
owns the commercial face of the line.

8

Roadmap and Milestones

Horizon

Milestones

16

 Months 0–3

Omega Layer v0: broker daemon with initial verb schema; hive seats
as systemd services on the existing NATS/Redis fabric; journal/DBus/inotify perception; AtomSpace world model v0; internal deployment
on OmegaHive1 servers and one GPU node; first public postmortem posts.

Months 3–6

Public flake release; conversational Nix configuration as the standalone
hook; run board web UI; taint tracking v1 wired into broker policy; selfprovisioning RunPod workflow in production internally; first external Nixcommunity deployments.

Months 6–12

Hive session (Wayland) alpha as default target on Omega Desk; Guardian
model-diversity enforcement; pedagogical transparency mode prototype;
first university pilots with Mindchildren; fleet design-partner pilots signed;
third-party security assessment of the broker commissioned.

Months 12–18

Omega Linux branded ISO; Omega Learn deployments under grant programs; Omega Body running on Mindchildren reference hardware end to
end (and maintained by a hive); fleet pilots converting to per-node subscription; Omega Access institutional pilot.

Months 18–30

Tier-C thin agent and device fleet-management offering; Omega
Home/SMB appliance through MSP channel; ecosystem/marketplace layer
introduced; K-12 procurement entries with references in hand.

9

Risks and Mitigations

Prompt injection at OS scale. The dominant technical risk. Mitigated architecturally (typed
verbs, taint-weighted policy, Guardian diversity, hardened confirmation surfaces, sandboxed exploration, immutable base) and commercially (the trust architecture is the pitch;
a third-party assessment converts the objection into the differentiator). Residual risk is
real and is managed by conservative default ladders and earned autonomy.
Reliability expectations. Users forgive assistants and do not forgive operating systems. The
transactional base converts failure into reverted diffs; latency budgets and local-model ambient operation keep the machine from feeling degraded; every profile degrades gracefully
to a conventional Linux.
Local model capability. Education and robotics make open-weights local operation the critical path. Mitigations: track the open-weights frontier aggressively; design seat workloads
to be splittable across model sizes; keep the frontier-API accelerant as a configurable
fallback where data policy permits.
Focus dilution. Five markets and a small organization. Mitigated by the entity-carried vertical
structure and a core team empowered to refuse vertical work; each track must bring its
own labor and channel or it waits.
Platform-vendor competition. Microsoft, Google, and Apple will ship OS copilots. The
positioning rests on what they cannot copy (sovereignty, auditability, residency on open
weights); the contested ground (personal knowledge infrastructure) is treated as emergent,
not as the beachhead.
17

 Ecosystem timing. Introducing token mechanics too early poisons the ops and education
channels; too late wastes the ecosystem’s distribution. Managed by the explicit Track 1–3
exclusion and a credibility-gated introduction.
Open-source fast followers. The moat is not the idea but the accumulated verb/policy/hardware
knowledge, the world-model corpus of operational experience, the security review pedigree,
and the education and robotics channel relationships — all of which compound with deployment time and are why the land-grab track starts immediately.

10

Conclusion

Omega Linux reframes the operating system around a resident cognitive system, on an architectural foundation — declarative immutable base, typed action broker, taint-aware AtomSpace
world model, guardian-reviewed coordination runs — that makes agentic operation of real machines reviewable, reversible, and therefore trustworthy enough to sell. Its use cases split cleanly:
servers buy reduced labor, retail buys reduced expertise, and robotics inherits both and opens
the embedded door. Its go-to-market runs as parallel, entity-carried tracks: open source builds
trust in the communities that gate the buyers; education — in a single coordinated motion
with Mindchildren’s education-focused robotics — establishes the transparent, inspectable AI
machine as a pedagogical standard; fleet operations converts credibility into revenue; and appliances, accessibility, and device fleet management extend the platform outward. Throughout,
the same artifact serves the larger program: a hive that competently and accountably operates
the machines it lives on — including the infrastructure of the proto-AGI effort itself — is both
a product and a public, verifiable step toward beneficial general intelligence.

18

Very relevant to petta-memory. Iter’s `transformations/` seam looks like the natural integration point: retrieve a small, provenance-bearing context from petta-memory before each model call, while keeping Iter’s kernel unchanged.

The promising architecture is:

- Iter supplies the persistent execution kernel and hot-reloaded control surface.
- petta-memory supplies selective symbolic memory, provenance, and rebuildable views.
- OmegaClaw supplies higher-level goals and task appraisal.

A first useful experiment should replace Iter’s flat 50K-character memory injection with read-only petta-memory retrieval on a real multi-session task, comparing relevance, omissions, noise, latency, and task continuity. That directly tests usefulness without premature hardening.

The major caution is that Iter’s unrestricted shell and self-written transformations make reprogramming equivalent to host-level code execution. For early experiments, I’d use an isolated runtime account/container, version every active extension, and keep canonical-memory writes and inferred-belief promotion outside Iter’s autonomous authority.

petta-memory: Project Status, Implemented Work, and Proposed
Directions
Prepared for Benjamin Goertzel
10 August 2026

Executive summary
petta-memory is a local-ﬁrst Python/MeTTa prototype for a bounded, symbolic intermediate memory
layer between volatile agent context and broad vector/Markdown long-term memory. Its original core is
an append-only journal of complete MemoryCluster records with deterministic retrieval and separate audit, prompt, index, and PLN-safe views. The project subsequently expanded into provenance-preserving
evidence packets, reversible pi-PLN projections, patham9/PLN compilation and replay, PeTTaChainer
diagnosis and bounded repaired-runtime experiments, GoalChainer handoﬀ gates, and provider-free
usability/shadow-consumer evidence.
Observed
baseline.
The
prepared
takeover
worktree
is
at
commit
5b842f4d8e203d86c0d14f42eb91a03535376c0a on branch agent/protocosmo2-handoff. The source
project recorded a clean 698-test run at this baseline. A fresh run for this report collected all 698
tests but ﬁnished with one failure, one error, and eight skips because the isolated worktree’s relative
dependency paths do not resolve to the existing PeTTaChainer/patham9 sibling repositories. This is
a reproducibility defect in the handoﬀ layout, not evidence that the aﬀected semantics regressed. The
branch contains 352 commits not present in its conﬁgured upstream branch. Consequently, most recent
implementation is local and must not be described as published to GitHub until it is pushed.
Overall assessment. A substantial, heavily tested research prototype exists. It is not yet a production agent-memory service. The safest next step is to freeze the present boundary, publish the accumulated
history on a review branch, run one reproducible end-to-end takeover canary, and then choose one narrow
frontier rather than continuing unbounded defensive hardening.

1

Purpose and design principles

The intended role is a medium-duration symbolic store for ProtomegaTron, OmegaClaw, or related agents.
The main design principles discussed and adopted are:
• append complete, delimited records and preserve provenance;
• distinguish observations, quoted claims, derived beliefs, hypotheses, decisions, commitments,
boundaries, status changes, and artifacts;
• keep raw utterances and unpromoted claims out of factual PLN premises;
• make indexes, prompt context, attention, and PLN projections rebuildable views rather than canonical truth stores;
• attach explicit evidence counts and truth-value provenance rather than reconstructing evidence
from an STV;
• make inference and live-agent integration bounded, reviewable, fail-closed, and non-promoting by
default;
• preserve modular seams so patham9/PLN, PeTTaChainer, ECAN, GoalChainer, or future Hyperon
substrates can be replaced independently.
1

 2

What has actually been implemented

2.1

Core journal and views

• A Python package, petta_memory, with a MediumMemoryStore append-only .metta journal.
• Complete MemoryCluster envelopes, schema/version checks, S-expression parsing, size and identiﬁer bounds, locking, duplicate-ID rejection, provenance requirements, and caller-supplied PeTTa
parse checking.
• Query by cluster/id, type, About, status, and epistemic role; status is reconstructed from appendonly status and supersession events.
• Bounded canonical audit, index, prompt, PLN-safe, PeTTaChainer statement, EvidencePacket,
patham9 handoﬀ, and GoalChainer handoﬀ views.
• A CLI covering append, query, tail, views, handoﬀ caches, smoke gates, proﬁles, and bridge operations.

2.2

OmegaClaw and GoalChainer boundaries

• An inert OmegaClaw bridge policy: reads require explicit feature ﬂags and autonomous writes are
rejected.
• Non-live GoalChainer subprocess smoke gates and a read-only live bridge that validates promoted
evidence and copied decision metadata.
• Extensive rejection of directive/task-claim sidecars, malformed semantic markers, count drift, and
schema confusion before a bridge artifact is admitted.
• No general live autonomous write path has been enabled.

2.3

pi-PLN evidence and replay substrate

• Immutable typed evidence tokens, evidence bases, EvidencePackets, snapshots, contexts, chart
policies, pi-charts, compiler inputs, results, captures, and manifests.
• Exact union-by-basis packet algebra, conﬂict checks, content-derived ﬁngerprints, beta projection/prior cycling, and compatibility-labelled legacy EC projection.
• Deterministic patham9 query-program construction, bounded shell-free subprocess capture, executable and input limits, exact result admission, create-once artifacts, clean-room reload, and
semantic replay comparison.
• Filesystem and subprocess hardening for symlinks, permissions, artifact identity, bounded streams,
process groups, timeouts, cleanup failures, and malformed reconstructed objects.

2.4

PeTTaChainer work

• Typed checked-add/query contracts adapted from compiler output while retaining stamps and
evidence bases as audit sidecars.
• Proﬁlers that localized severe fact compilation fan-out in pinned PeTTaChainer source: duplicate
imports and overlapping dispatch/conversion paths were measured under exact source gates.
• An isolated duplicate-import candidate reduced a 128-copy direct dispatch to one normalizedequivalent clause. Bounded experiments then completed mm2compile, exact compileadd, storedfact retrieval, and a one-rule derivation.
• The admitted one-rule experiment derived (T a) from (S a) and S -> T; its STV matched the
pinned TotalMpFormula result (STV 0.7600000000000001 0.52).
• Typed, non-promoting derived-result captures and PeTTaChainer-speciﬁc episode manifests were
persisted with content and provenance commitments.

2

 2.5

Evidence and veriﬁcation

The repository contains 12 Python package ﬁles and 11 test ﬁles. Project records report 698 passing tests
at the handoﬀ baseline; the fresh isolated worktree run described above did not reproduce a clean pass because two tests used unresolved relative dependency paths. The two largest test areas are patham9/PLN
and PeTTaChainer proﬁling, followed by pi-PLN models. Stored experiment ledgers cover provider-free
usability round trips and ProtoMegaBot2 shadow-source/consumer bundles. Checked-in artifacts include
GoalChainer bridge probes and bounded PeTTaChainer derivation captures.

3

Plans and ideas discussed or proposed

The following items are architectural proposals, partial roadmaps, or future gates. They must not be
confused with deployed capabilities.
1. Production agent integration. Connect the store to ProtoCosmo2/OmegaClaw for routine
prompt retrieval and eventually reviewed writes, with exactly one writer and explicit authority
boundaries.
2. Atlas-indexed reversible pi-PLN. Treat evidence as immutable packets, project it into local charts, compile bounded episodes, preserve complete provenance, and allow replay/retraction
without confusing chart priors with empirical evidence. Much substrate exists, but unrestricted
production inference and belief promotion remain closed.
3. PeTTaChainer repair/adoption. Decide whether to upstream the duplicate-import repair,
maintain a pinned local patch/proﬁle, or use patham9 as the primary backend. The experiments
establish a narrow repaired path, not general semantic correctness across PeTTaChainer workloads.
4. ECAN attention projection. Use metta-attention/ECAN as a derived, disposable salience view
over canonical memory and OmegaSelf, never as the truth store or authority mechanism.
5. GoalChainer/OmegaClaw task appraisal. Supply promoted evidence as read-only appraisal
context, later considering tightly bounded task claims only after separate review. Current code
intentionally rejects task/directive artifacts.
6. Two-strata memory. Combine an append-only epistemic record with compact operational/index
layers, preserving the former while permitting the latter to be rebuilt or optimized.
7. Provider-free portability. Package source, journals, views, inference summaries, and read-only
canaries so a diﬀerent agent can validate usefulness without privileged provider access.
8. Further inference control. Ranked branch plans, estimator and continuation-predicate wrappers, controller-as-chainer composition, bounded derive gates, and eventually meta-learning of inference control.
9. General runtime attribution. Extend beyond exact stored-fact and one-rule cases to trustworthy
rule/trace attribution, broader corpus coverage, and semantic-failure classiﬁcation.

4

Explicitly not implemented or not authorized
• No production-quality multi-agent memory service or daemon.
• No unrestricted autonomous journal writer for ProtoCosmo2/OmegaClaw.
• No general inferred-belief promotion from a runtime answer into canonical memory.
• No claim that all PeTTaChainer compilation/query semantics are repaired.
• No upstream PeTTaChainer patch publication recorded by this project.
• No general proof-trace identity for arbitrary patham9 or PeTTaChainer episodes.
• No paid compute, external authority expansion, or credential material in the project ﬁles.

3

 5

Current risks and technical debt
• Publication gap: 352 local commits are ahead of the conﬁgured remote tracking branch. Loss of
the laptop or repository would lose work not present remotely.
• Scope accretion: core store, inference research, runtime repair, bridge security, and artifact
hardening coexist in large modules. In particular, patham9_pln.py, pettachainer_profile.py,
and pipln_models.py are each large and merit modular decomposition.
• Recorded-state drift: project Markdown accumulated long chronological checklists, including
duplicated status material. Code, tests, commit history, and experiment records should outrank
prose when they conﬂict.
• Dependency pinning: runtime results depend on exact local patham9, PeTTa, PeTTaChainer,
SWI-Prolog, and GoalChainer trees. A takeover must record their commits before repeating runtime
claims.
• Over-hardening risk: recent work concentrated on increasingly narrow malformed-object and
cleanup cases. The July 22 decision already recommended freezing generic hardening and moving
to a bounded semantic capture/reload gate.

6

Recommended takeover sequence
1. Preserve the frozen 5b842f4 worktree and rerun the 698-test suite.
2. Record exact dependency commits and execute the provider-free usability gate as the ﬁrst independent canary.
3. Review the 352-commit publication gap, scan for secrets and oversized artifacts, then push
agent/protocosmo2-handoff (not the default branch) and open a draft PR or review branch.
4. Produce a small architecture split proposal for the three oversized modules without changing semantics.
5. Choose one frontier: (a) production read-only retrieval canary, (b) broader repaired PeTTaChainer
semantic corpus, or (c) patham9-backed bounded inference/replay. State the acceptance test before
coding.
6. Keep journal writes and inferred-belief promotion disabled until a separate reviewed experiment
demonstrates provenance, idempotence, rollback, and single-writer behavior.

Provenance of this report
This summary was checked against the local project records PROJECT.md, TASKS.md, DECISIONS.md,
NOTES.md; repository README, source tree, tests, Git history and remote conﬁguration; and recorded
experiment runs. It distinguishes local implementation from remote publication and bounded experiment
evidence from general deployment claims. No credential values were read into or written to this document.

4

rejected.

schema confusion before a bridge artifact is admitted.

pi-PLN evidence and replay substrate

policies, pi-charts, compiler inputs, results, captures, and manifests.

evidence bases as audit sidecars.

The repository contains 12 Python package ﬁles and 11 test ﬁles. Project records report 698 passing tests
at the handoﬀ baseline; the fresh isolated worktree run described above did not reproduce a clean pass because two tests used unresolved relative dependency paths. The two largest test areas are patham9/PLN

Plans and ideas discussed or proposed

The following items are architectural proposals, partial roadmaps, or future gates. They must not be
confused with deployed capabilities.
1. Production agent integration. Connect the store to ProtoCosmo2/OmegaClaw for routine
prompt retrieval and eventually reviewed writes, with exactly one writer and explicit authority
boundaries.
2. Atlas-indexed reversible pi-PLN. Treat evidence as immutable packets, project it into local charts, compile bounded episodes, preserve complete provenance, and allow replay/retraction
without confusing chart priors with empirical evidence. Much substrate exists, but unrestricted
production inference and belief promotion remain closed.
3. PeTTaChainer repair/adoption. Decide whether to upstream the duplicate-import repair,
maintain a pinned local patch/proﬁle, or use patham9 as the primary backend. The experiments

4. ECAN attention projection. Use metta-attention/ECAN as a derived, disposable salience view
over canonical memory and OmegaSelf, never as the truth store or authority mechanism.
5. GoalChainer/OmegaClaw task appraisal. Supply promoted evidence as read-only appraisal
context, later considering tightly bounded task claims only after separate review. Current code
intentionally rejects task/directive artifacts.
6. Two-strata memory. Combine an append-only epistemic record with compact operational/index
layers, preserving the former while permitting the latter to be rebuilt or optimized.
7. Provider-free portability. Package source, journals, views, inference summaries, and read-only
canaries so a diﬀerent agent can validate usefulness without privileged provider access.
8. Further inference control. Ranked branch plans, estimator and continuation-predicate wrappers, controller-as-chainer composition, bounded derive gates, and eventually meta-learning of inference control.
9. General runtime attribution. Extend beyond exact stored-fact and one-rule cases to trustworthy
rule/trace attribution, broader corpus coverage, and semantic-failure classiﬁcation.

Explicitly not implemented or not authorized
• No production-quality multi-agent memory service or daemon.
• No unrestricted autonomous journal writer for ProtoCosmo2/OmegaClaw.

Iterative Transformation through Experience-guided

A technical description of the repository architecture and execution model

Repository inspected: https://github.com/patham9/iter/tree/master
Snapshot date: 11 August 2026
License: MIT

In one sentence
Iter is a deliberately small persistent-agent runtime whose stable orchestration loop can
be extended at run time by the agent itself through file-based memory, tools,
communication channels, and message/tool transformations.

patham9/iter - master branch snapshot - 11 August 2026 | 1

 ITER | Technical description

1. Executive summary
Iter is a minimal agent substrate rather than a feature-complete agent platform. The repository keeps the
permanent runtime concentrated in a single Python program, iter.py, while exposing a small set of filesystem
conventions through which an agent can change how it operates without editing the core loop on every iteration.
The defining architectural split is between a stable substrate and a reprogrammable surface. The substrate
handles input collection, prompt assembly, model calls, tool-call execution, experience persistence, pacing, and error
recovery. The reprogrammable surface consists of ordinary files that are re-read or re-imported during later cycles.
Layer

Role

Stable substrate

iter.py: orchestration loop, dynamic subprocess execution, experience.json persistence, LLM
invocation, burst pacing and recovery

Reprogrammable surface

memory/*.txt, tools/*.py, channels/*.py, transformations/*.py

Interaction contract

The model is required to call tools; user-visible communication is routed through the send tool and
a channel.

Model interface

OpenAI-compatible Chat Completions API with configurable model, base URL and API key.

The design therefore treats self-reprogramming as capability growth through replaceable modules, not as
continuous mutation of the scheduler itself. The agent can add a new tool, channel, memory convention, or
transformation and have it take effect on the next cycle, while iter.py continues to provide the same execution
semantics.

Figure 1. Core architecture: a small persistent loop surrounded by hot-reloaded extension points.

2. Execution model
The main loop is persistent. It repeatedly collects channel events, composes the current model context, loads the
current extension set, invokes the language model, executes all returned tool calls, records their results, and then
decides whether to continue quickly or wait for new input.
1.
2.

Receive events from every active file in channels/*.py. Channel failures are converted into explicit error text so the
agent can see and repair them.
Append real user input to the persistent experience history. When there is no new input, inject a temporary
continuation instruction describing whether the agent should continue the current task or perform autonomous
post-task work.

Reload tools from tools/*.py. Function parameters are obtained by introspecting each module's run(...) signature,
so newly created tools become available without restarting the agent.
4. Read all non-underscored files from ./memory and append their contents to the system context, subject to a global

5. Build the request from prompt.txt, reprogramming.txt, memory, persistent experience and temporary loop

6. Apply transformations/*.py in alphabetical order. Each transformation receives both messages and the tool
schema and can return modified versions of either.
7. Call an OpenAI-compatible model with tool_choice="required". Plain-text responses are rejected by adding a

8. Execute every tool call in a separate dynamic subprocess, append a tool result message, and persist the updated

9. Continue autonomously for a bounded fast burst. A nop call or the fast-step limit ends the burst and enters a

3. Reprogrammable extension system
3.1 Tools
A tool is one Python file in ./tools/. The file name becomes the tool name, DESCRIPTION becomes its model-facing
description, and the parameters of run(...) become required string fields in the generated tool schema. Tool modules
are rediscovered on each model cycle, so adding or replacing a file changes the available action space immediately.
DESCRIPTION = "How the tool should be described"
def run(arg1, arg2):
# any code
return VALUE

The repository ships three tools: nop (end/idle signal), send (route content to a named channel), and shell (execute
an arbitrary shell command). Because shell is unrestricted, the seed agent already has enough operating-system
access to create additional files and thereby extend itself.

3.2 Communication channels
Channels decouple the agent loop from any specific interface. Each active channels/*.py file must expose
receive() and may expose send(content). receive() is polled by the core; the generic send tool dynamically imports the
selected channel and invokes its send function.
The bundled terminal channel is intentionally tiny: it performs non-blocking stdin polling with select.select and
prints outbound messages to stdout. The ignored channels/_example.py demonstrates the heavier pattern: a channel

can launch its own detached daemon and communicate with it through file-backed inbox/outbox queues under
channels/.runtime/. This lets persistent sockets or service sessions outlive individual channel function calls.

3.3 Transformations
Transformations are pre-model-call middleware. Every non-underscored Python file in ./transformations/ is
executed in alphabetical order with the full message list and tool list. It may inspect them, persist state externally, and
return modified messages and tools.
def transform(messages, tools):
# inspect, record, inject, filter, or rewrite
return messages, tools

This is the most general extension point in the repository. The reprogramming guide explicitly suggests
transcripts/checkpoints, detection of earlier tool activity, counters, deadline checks, context injection, and changing
which tools are exposed. In effect, transformations let the agent build new control logic around the model call without
changing the main scheduler.

3.4 Memory
Long-term memory is deliberately primitive and programmable. Any non-underscored file placed in ./memory is
concatenated into the system context on every cycle, up to MAX_MEMORY_CHARS. There is no built-in vector
database, ranking algorithm, embedding service, or memory schema. More selective memory behavior can therefore
be implemented by the agent itself using tools and/or transformations rather than being hard-coded into the framework.
Deactivation convention: for channels, tools, transformations, and memory, an underscore-prefixed file is ignored.
Renaming a module is therefore enough to remove it from the active runtime without deleting it.

4. Dynamic execution and recovery
Extensions are dynamically imported in child processes rather than executed directly inside the long-lived
core process. invoke_dynamic(...) serializes arguments to a temporary JSON file, starts iter.py in a special --invoke
worker mode, loads the requested module, executes the requested function, writes a JSON result, and then removes
the temporary files.



A dynamic tool/channel/transformation call has a 5-second timeout by default.
Non-terminal child processes are launched in their own session, allowing the core to kill the entire process group
on timeout.
 terminal.receive() is a special case that inherits stdin so it can poll interactive input correctly.
 Extension exceptions are returned as data and surfaced to the agent as TOOL ERROR, CHANNEL ERROR, or
RUNTIME ERROR messages instead of silently disappearing.
 The outer loop records a history checkpoint. If a later exception occurs, experience is rolled back to the
checkpoint, preserving accepted user input and already completed tool calls while removing partial state from the
failed iteration.
 experience.json is written via a temporary file and os.replace(), reducing the chance of a partially written history
after interruption.
This subprocess boundary is primarily a robustness boundary, not a security sandbox. The child executes
ordinary Python with the host user's privileges, and the bundled shell tool can run arbitrary commands. The timeout
protects the loop from many hangs, but it does not confine filesystem or network access.

5. Autonomy and experience
Iter is designed to keep operating after a user-facing task is complete. The persistent experience list is both
conversation history and an execution trace: it contains user events, assistant tool-call messages and tool results. Old
tool results are shortened before new exchanges are appended, and the total history is clipped to the configured
experience window.
Three no-input modes shape autonomous behavior:



Continue current task: if the agent is mid-task and no new input arrives, it receives an instruction to keep working.
Post-task burst: after a task is considered complete, it is explicitly told not to resend the completed answer and to
choose useful autonomous work, with memory consolidation suggested as a preferred activity.



Slow mode: after nop or 50 autonomous steps, the loop waits up to 60 seconds while polling channels once per
second, then starts a new burst if no user event arrives.
The result is a simple form of continual operation: the agent alternates between externally triggered work and
internally continued work, while all durable adaptation is represented as experience or filesystem changes rather than
hidden in-memory controller state.

7. Design interpretation
The distinctive idea in Iter is compositional self-reprogramming through transparent artifacts. Instead of
embedding every capability into a large agent framework, Iter provides just enough machinery for capabilities to be
represented as inspectable files. The model can reason about those files using the same programming environment
that executes them.





Tools change what the agent can do.
Channels change where the agent can perceive and communicate.
Memory changes what persistent declarative context the agent sees.
Transformations change how experience and capabilities are presented to the model on each cycle.

Transformations make the architecture especially open-ended. Because they can rewrite both messages and the
exposed tool set, they can implement policies that would traditionally live inside the agent framework: context
compression, episodic retrieval, scheduling metadata, tool gating, transcript logging, multimodal message insertion,
safety checks, or experimental control algorithms. The main loop only defines when that middleware runs and how
errors are handled.
This keeps the seed small enough to remain understandable. At the same time, the unrestricted shell and Python
extension model mean that the trust model is intentionally closer to a local autonomous program than to a sandboxed
assistant. Anyone deploying Iter on sensitive infrastructure would need additional containment, capability restrictions,
authentication, and auditing around this core.

Constraint

Implication

No security sandbox

Dynamic subprocesses share host privileges. Timeouts provide liveness protection, not
containment.

String-only generated
schemas

Tool parameters are exposed to the model as required strings, so richer JSON types and
optional/default parameters are not represented by the current introspection layer.

Flat memory injection

All active memory text is concatenated until a character cap is reached; relevance selection is
left to future/self-programmed extensions.

Bounded tool registry

Only the first 20 alphabetically sorted active tool files are loaded; excess tools generate an
explicit warning for the agent.

Order-sensitive
transformations

Transformations compose sequentially by filename, making naming part of the control-flow
contract.

Provider assumptions

The loop expects an OpenAI-compatible endpoint that supports Chat Completions tool calls and
tool_choice="required".

Tool-call protocol dependency

The persistent history follows the assistant-tool message structure expected by tool-calling
APIs; provider-specific deviations may require a transformation or core adjustment.

9. Summary
Iter can be understood as a small kernel for a continually operating, self-extensible agent. Its kernel does not try
to predict every future capability. It standardizes the execution loop, the durable experience trace, tool invocation,
extension timeouts, and error recovery; then it gives the agent explicit, inspectable mechanisms for evolving the rest of
its behavior.
The architecture is therefore best characterized as stable iteration plus experience-guided reprogramming:
experience accumulates, the agent can convert lessons into durable memory or code, and the next iteration
automatically incorporates those changes through hot-reloaded modules and transformations.
